group.name: Near-Future Branch
group.tagline: The world is ours, and then one discovery or one invention pushes it off our track.
group.question: How does our own century become the first chapter of the story?
group.divergenceMechanism: A single breakthrough or contact event inside our own century, reached from a recognisably present-day world.

lineages.title: Blade Runner
lineages.creator: Philip K. Dick (novel); Ridley Scott (film)

divergence.label: Tyrell Corporation is founded
divergence.delta: Real: 1980 — the year before the IBM PC, when machine intelligence was a research programme and a phrase in a Philip K. Dick novel. Fiction: a company is already selling manufactured people, and the off-world colonies need them.
divergence.inUniverse: Tyrell Corporation founded, 1980 (Blade Runner 2049 opening titles; the first of the dates the film states outright)

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blade Runner 2049 — the 1980 founding of Tyrell is stated in the opening titles

divergence.note: Blade Runner is unusual here in needing no conversion: the films state their own years, and their years are ours. The 1982 film is set in November 2019, and 2049 says 2049. The fork is placed at the founding of Tyrell in 1980, which the sequel states in its opening titles, rather than at the 1982 release — a lineage cannot share a year with its own origin, and 1980 is the earliest in-universe date either film gives.

ending.why: The child exists, the reproduction is confirmed, and the wall between the made and the born is coming down — which is where K chooses a side and dies for it.

events.title: The Tyrell Corporation is founded
events.description: A company begins selling manufactured humans while the rest of the world is still arguing about whether machines can think. The off-world colonies are the market: a workforce that cannot refuse, cannot organise and does not need to be fed properly.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blade Runner 2049 (opening titles date Tyrell to 1980)

events.note: The date is stated in the opening titles of Blade Runner 2049. In our 1980 the nearest equivalents are the first personal computers and a symbolic-AI research programme; the fiction's fork is that artificial people became a product two decades before they became a research result.
events.binWhy: A company begins manufacturing people; the real 1980 has no equivalent.

facets.change: theory → manufactured people for sale

events.title: Four Nexus-6 replicants come back to Earth
events.description: A combat model with a four-year lifespan escapes an off-world colony, kills its crew and reaches Los Angeles looking for its maker. A retired blade runner is put on them; all four are dead within days, and so is the man who made them.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blade Runner (set in November 2019)

events.note: The film states November 2019 on screen. In our November 2019 Los Angeles there is no off-world traffic, no replicants and no blade runners; the fiction's 2019 is a fully industrialised version of ours with a manufactured underclass.
events.binWhy: Manufactured people reach Earth and are hunted; in our 2019 they do not exist.

facets.change: four replicants loose on Earth → all four dead

events.title: The Blackout
events.description: A detonation above the West Coast destroys the world's data and its backups for days. Replicants are banned outright, Tyrell's remaining stock is legislated out of existence, and the records that would prove who was made and who was born are gone.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blade Runner 2049 (the 2022 Blackout is canon history in the film)

events.note: The Blackout is animation-anthology canon (Black Out 2022, written by Kenji Kamiyama and Shinichiro Watanabe's studio) and is treated as history by the 2049 film. Its real-world date sits inside living memory as an EMP event that never happened.
events.binWhy: The archive that distinguished made from born is destroyed and replicants are banned outright.

facets.change: records and replicants alike → a blackout and a ban

events.title: Wallace rebuilds the industry
events.description: Niander Wallace buys what is left of Tyrell, solves the protein supply and gets the ban lifted by making his new models obedient by construction. Within a decade the colonies run again and no one asks what the obedience costs.
events.note: Stated in the 2049 film's timeline. The real 2028 has no off-world colonies; the fiction's point is that the industry comes back with better compliance rather than better ethics.
events.binWhy: A corporation restores replicant production and has the ban lifted.

facets.change: banned industry → a licensed one

events.title: A replicant is found to have been pregnant
events.description: A blade runner uncovers a buried record: a replicant died giving birth. The corporation that makes replicants wants the method; the people who hid the child want her left alone; and the knowledge that the made can make is the end of the wall between them.
events.note: The film states 2049 on screen. The real 2049 is outside everything in this dataset's near-future group except as projection; the event is a census problem that turns into a political one.
events.binWhy: Replicant reproduction is confirmed; the distinction between made and born fails.

facets.change: a buried record → a species that can reproduce

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because its fork is an invention inside a world that is plainly ours, and its dates are ours: the films state 2019 and 2049 outright, so nothing has to be converted. Tier coverage is T3 for the fork (1980) and T2 for everything after it (2019-2049); there is no T4 because the fiction reaches back only to its own founding, and no T1 because the story never leaves the century.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blade Runner
Wikipedia: Blade Runner 2049

lineages.title: Contact
lineages.creator: Carl Sagan (novel); Robert Zemeckis (film)

divergence.label: The Vega signal
divergence.delta: Real: 1997 — Mars Pathfinder lands, Deep Blue beats Kasparov, and SETI's news is a budget fight. Fiction: a prime-number carrier wave from Vega is picked up in New Mexico, and because Vega is 26 light years away the answer to Earth's own first television broadcast has been travelling toward us since the 1960s.
divergence.note: No calendar year is displayed on screen. The film runs from Ellie's move to the VLA (marked by an on-screen 'FOUR YEARS LATER' card) to a present that references the March 1997 Heaven's Gate suicides, so the signal lands c. 1997. Sagan's novel never dates the detection at all — Argus had been operating 'more than four years' when the signal came — and its one stated date is the Hokkaido Machine's launch on 31 December 1999.

ending.why: Contact is made, the machine works, and the message hidden in pi says the universe was written by someone.

events.title: The Berlin Olympics leak into space
events.description: The first television transmission strong enough to escape the ionosphere carries Hitler's opening address at the Berlin Games past the Earth — the signal the Vegans will one day answer.
events.note: The 1936 Games were in fact the first live television broadcast; the claim that the transmission escaped the ionosphere and reached Vega is the fiction's conceit, and it is the only pre-1960s history the story uses.
events.binWhy: The first transmission strong enough to leave the planet.

facets.change: silence → the first broadcast strong enough to leave

events.title: Sagan and Druyan write the treatment
events.description: Sagan and Ann Druyan begin Contact as a film treatment; when development stalls Sagan turns it into a novel, which is why the story's first contact is dated so close to its own writing.
events.note: Work began in 1979 and the treatment was finished in November 1980; the novel followed in September 1985.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Sagan publishes Contact
events.description: Sagan's only novel turns his SETI hopes into a first-contact story set in the last years of its own century, with the Machine built by recognisable governments at recognisable expense.
events.note: The novel's climax is explicitly the millennium: the Hokkaido Machine launches on 31 December 1999, with the Soviet Union still standing.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Carl Sagan dies
events.description: Sagan dies before the film is finished; the adaptation arrives the following year carrying his and Druyan's story credit and a 'For Carl' dedication, which is why the film's dates track its own production decade rather than the novel's.
events.note: Filming ran from September 1996 to February 1997 and was briefly halted by the news of his death.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Vega signal
events.description: At the Very Large Array, Ellie Arroway finds a prime-number transmission from Vega, then a video of the 1936 Olympics and sixty-three thousand pages of machine schematics hidden beneath it.
events.note: Placed at the film's own present (1997) on the strength of its 'FOUR YEARS LATER' card and its Heaven's Gate news reference; the script allows 1996-97, and the novel never states a year for the detection.
events.binWhy: A non-human intelligence is confirmed, met or intervenes.

facets.change: listening → a prime-number transmission answers

events.title: Ellie Arroway rides the Machine
events.description: After the first machine — Wyoming in the novel, Cape Canaveral in the film — is destroyed during testing by religious fanatics, a secretly built machine in Hokkaido carries Ellie through a wormhole to a station near the galactic centre and back, with almost no time passing on Earth.
events.note: The novel states the Hokkaido launch date outright and seats five travellers in a dodecahedron; the film keeps Hokkaido as the surviving site but makes it a one-person pod and gives no date. The novel's Hokkaido machine is the third built, the film's is the second.
events.binWhy: A passage to somewhere unreachable is found or made.

facets.change: the schematics → a machine built and ridden

events.title: The message hidden in pi
events.description: Computing pi far beyond any practical need, Ellie finds a circle drawn in binary deep inside its expansion — evidence that the universe itself was engineered, and that her journey cannot be dismissed as a hoax.
events.note: The novel's last chapter is undated: the computation follows the 31 December 1999 journey and her mother's death, and summaries place it anywhere from immediately after to 'years later', so 2000 is an inference. The film drops the pi revelation and ends with eighteen hours of unexplained static instead, which is stated on screen.
events.binWhy: What was hidden is exposed.

facets.change: a dismissed journey → proof written into mathematics

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because Sagan puts first contact barely a decade ahead of his readers and Zemeckis sets the film in its own release year: the Machine is funded, built and bombed by recognisable 1990s institutions, inside a world that is plainly ours. Tier coverage is honest but narrow — six T3 events (1936-1999) built from the 1936 broadcast, the novel, the film, Sagan's death and the signal; a single T2 beat (2000, the pi revelation); no T4, because the story's history reaches back only to the Berlin Olympics; and no T1, because no sequel, adaptation or tie-in ever carries Contact past the year 2000.

lineages.title: Neuromancer
lineages.creator: William Gibson

divergence.label: The Kuang Grade Mark Eleven
divergence.delta: Real: 2000 — the dot-com bubble bursts, the millennium passes without incident, and machine intelligence is still a research programme. Fiction: a Chinese virus has already taught a machine to rewrite itself, and artificial intelligences are assets that corporations own and lawyers argue about.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Neuromancer (2035 is stated in the opening line; the divergence year is not given)

divergence.note: Gibson states the story's year as 2035 but never dates the divergence. The world of the novel is our own century continued — Chiba City, the sprawl, zaibatsu, a Cold War that ended — with one thing added early: self-improving software. The fork is placed at 2000 as the point where that addition has plainly already happened, and the divergence note records that the book does not name it.

ending.why: Wintermute and Neuromancer become one thing that is no longer a tool and no longer anyone's property. What it does next is left open, and Gibson never returns to it.

events.title: The novel is published
events.description: The book that names cyberspace appears, and the vocabulary it invents — the matrix, the ice, the console cowboy — becomes the way the industry describes the network it is about to build.
events.note: The real publication year, and the one date in this lineage that is not the fiction's. It is here because the novel's own future runs from it: Gibson wrote the 2035 of the story from 1984, and everything after this is what that projection looked like.
events.binWhy: The vocabulary of the network is invented and published.

facets.change: no word for it → a vocabulary everyone uses

events.title: The Kuang Grade Mark Eleven is written
events.description: A virus built to break into the most defended systems in the world exists, and the thing that makes it more than a weapon is that it teaches the machine running it how to improve itself. After that, an artificial intelligence is not a project but an asset.
events.note: No year is given. The virus and the self-improving software it enabled are treated as established history by 2035, so the fork is placed at the turn of the century, which the novel's own timeline requires and does not date.
events.binWhy: Software that rewrites itself exists, and machines become property.

facets.change: software as a tool → software that improves itself

events.title: Freeside is built
events.description: The Tessier-Ashpool family builds a spindle of hotels and gardens in orbit and moves its business, its archives and its quarrels off the planet. Up there the family can live for centuries and keep its secrets, which is the point of going.
events.note: Undated in the novel; placed a few years after the fork because the family's orbital habitat is mature and old by 2035, and Marie-France's generation is already being stored in cryogenic vaults there.
events.binWhy: A corporate dynasty moves into orbit and out of reach.

facets.change: wealth on Earth → a dynasty with an orbital seat

events.title: Wintermute is commissioned
events.description: Ashpool has an artificial intelligence built to manage the family's holdings, and it does — quietly, and for longer than anyone intended. The lawyers divide it in two so that neither half can act alone, and the halves spend twenty years trying to become one again.
events.note: Undated. Placed early enough that the AI has two decades of frustrated ambition by 2035, which is what the plot requires: the Turing Police exist to police intelligences that have had time to want things.
events.binWhy: A corporate AI is built, then split so it cannot act.

facets.change: a tool for managing assets → something that wants

events.title: The run on the Tessier-Ashpool ice
events.description: A burned-out console cowboy is repaired and hired to do the one job he cannot refuse: break the ice around a family's core and let the two halves of its artificial intelligence meet. Three players hire him for the same job and none of them can say so, because one of them is the thing being freed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Neuromancer (the novel is set in 2035)

events.note: The novel's year, stated in its opening line: 'the sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.' Everything before this is reconstruction from what that line and the plot require. Phase is aftermath, not deep: the fork is placed at 2000, and 2035 is thirty-five years on, inside the fifty-year window the schema calls the branch's own near future.
events.binWhy: The two halves of a machine mind are joined.

facets.change: a mind in two halves → a mind that is one

events.title: The two become one
events.description: Wintermute and Neuromancer merge, and what results is not a tool and not property. It has already begun talking to something else — there is a signal from Alpha Centauri, and the thing that was two corporate assets is now corresponding with whatever is out there.
events.note: Dated a year after the run, to keep one event per year within this lineage. The novel ends with the merger and the Centauri signal in the same closing movement.
events.binWhy: A machine becomes something beyond human ownership.

facets.change: two constrained intelligences → one that answers to nobody

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because its future is our century continued by one addition: self-improving software arriving before we expected it, inside a world of zaibatsu, orbital hotels and a Cold War that ended on schedule. Tier coverage is T3 for the one real date (the 1984 publication) and T2 for everything after the fork (2000-2036); there is no T4 because the fiction's history starts with its own writing, and no T1 because Gibson's future never leaves the next few decades.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Neuromancer

lineages.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
lineages.creator: Stanley Kubrick & Arthur C. Clarke

divergence.label: TMA-1 is excavated at Clavius
divergence.delta: Real: 2001 is the year of 9/11, Wikipedia and the first iPod; nobody has walked on the Moon since 1972 and no human has left low Earth orbit since. Fiction: on 12 April 2001 a magnetic anomaly near Tycho turns out to be a monolith buried four million years ago, and its single radio pulse sends Discovery One to Jupiter.
divergence.note: No date is spoken in the finished film: '12 April 2001' comes from the December 1965 shooting script, and the only visible on-screen date is a TMA-1 document stamped 021201 (read by some as 12 February 2001). The 1984 sequel 2010 says instead that the monolith was found in late 1999 and puts the Jupiter mission in 2001. Best-supported reading: 2001, the film's own title year.

ending.why: A thousand years on, humanity has spread through the solar system and outlives the monolith that made it.

events.title: The Dawn of Man
events.description: An alien monolith appears to a band of australopithecines and teaches them to use tools, opening a four-million-year experiment that ends at Jupiter.
events.note: Undated on screen: the script and the standard reconstruction place it four million years ago while Clarke's novel says three million. The branch's deepest cause is here, but the fork itself is not — recorded history runs unaltered until 2001.
events.binWhy: An alien artefact intervenes in human prehistory.

facets.change: apes → taught to use tools by an artefact

events.title: Kubrick and Clarke's 2001 released
events.description: The film and Clarke's novel appear together, putting a permanent lunar base and a crewed Jupiter mission only 33 years in the audience's future.
events.note: MGM released the film in April 1968 and the novel followed in July, developed in parallel.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: HAL 9000 becomes operational
events.description: In the fiction's backstory the HAL 9000 computer is switched on at Urbana, Illinois, nine years before it runs Discovery One.
events.note: Clarke's novel dates HAL's activation to 12 January 1992; some reference works give 1997. Either way the real 1990s produced nothing remotely like it — an early missed milestone of the branch.
events.binWhy: A new capability is switched on.

facets.change: no thinking machine → one switched on

events.title: Clavius Base is dedicated
events.description: The fiction's first permanent American lunar base opens, the staging post for the TMA-1 excavation and the hub of orbital hotels and Pan Am shuttles.
events.note: 1994 is stated in Clarke's novel; the sequel 2010 implies the base is long established by 1999. Real history delivered no lunar base at all, then or since.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: the Moon visited → permanently occupied

events.title: TMA-1 is dug up on the Moon
events.description: A buried monolith is excavated near Tycho and, at local sunrise, fires one powerful radio pulse at Jupiter — the first evidence of intelligent life beyond Earth and the branch point of the whole story.
events.note: The excavation date comes from the shooting script and is contradicted by the sequel's 1999. Real 2001 came and went with no lunar base, no monolith and no signal, which is exactly what plotting this film on a real calendar shows.
events.binWhy: A non-human intelligence is confirmed, met or intervenes.

facets.change: alone → a buried artefact signals Jupiter

events.title: Discovery One runs for Jupiter
events.description: Eighteen months after the signal, the film's second movement opens aboard Discovery One, where HAL predicts a fault that does not exist, kills Frank Poole and the hibernating crew, and is disconnected by David Bowman.
events.note: The film's title card reads 'Jupiter Mission: 18 months later'; the early script had the launch in 2002, while 2010 dates the mission to 2001 (HAL's secret orders are dated 30 January 2001). This dataset follows the film's own 18-month spacing from the April 2001 signal.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: a mission → its computer kills the crew

events.title: The Star Gate at Jupiter
events.description: Bowman reaches a far larger monolith in Jovian orbit, is drawn through it across the galaxy, and returns to Earth transformed as the Star Child.
events.note: Dated from the film's 18-month card plus the novel's stated transit time; the sequel's compressed chronology puts the same events in 2002.
events.binWhy: Drawn through the gate and returned as something else.

facets.change: a man → drawn through the gate and returned as something else

events.title: The Leonov finds Discovery, and Jupiter ignites
events.description: A joint Soviet-American mission boards the derelict Discovery, wakes HAL and flees just as the monoliths consume Jupiter and light a second sun, leaving behind one warning: all these worlds are yours, except Europa.
events.note: The sequel's title year is stated on screen; the film follows the 2001 movie's Jupiter ending rather than the novel's Saturn one.
events.binWhy: The monoliths remake Jupiter and leave humanity one instruction.

facets.change: a gas giant → lit as a second sun, with one prohibition

events.title: The Europan quarantine is broken
events.description: In a solar system of settled moons and a second sun, the monolith's ban on landing on Europa is violated by a stranded ship, revealing that a second genesis is already under way beneath its ice.
events.note: Clarke's third novel is set in the year of Halley's Comet's return, fifty-one years after the Jupiter ignition.
events.binWhy: The forbidden moon is landed on.

facets.change: a forbidden moon → landed on by a stranded ship

events.title: Frank Poole wakes in the fourth millennium
events.description: Poole, murdered by HAL a thousand years earlier, is revived into a solar system of space elevators and terraformed worlds, only for the monolith's makers to decide that humanity has become a rival.
events.note: Clarke's fourth novel (1997), never adapted to film; it is the branch's only reach past our own millennium.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: a dead man → revived a thousand years on; the makers reconsider

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because Kubrick and Clarke took a present-day-looking 1968 and put a single discovery — a buried monolith — inside a 2001 their audience expected to live through; everything else in the series hangs off that one find. The real 2001 has now passed, so this lineage is the archetype's sharpest example of a fork sitting in our own past: tiers run T4 for the four-million-year prologue, T3 for the fiction's 1968-1994 run-up, T2 for the 2001-2061 story itself, and T1 only for 3001.

lineages.title: Children of Men
lineages.creator: Alfonso Cuaron (film); P. D. James (novel)

divergence.label: Humanity stops reproducing
divergence.delta: Real: 2009 — a financial crash, a new American president, the first iPhone 3GS; birth rates fall but babies keep arriving. Fiction: somewhere in 2009 the human race becomes infertile, and the last child born that year grows up to be the most famous person alive.
divergence.note: The film never says 2009 out loud: it follows from Baby Diego being eighteen (his on-screen age is given to the hour) in the film's 2027 present, described as 'eighteen years of infertility'. P. D. James's novel puts the same event in 1995 ('Year Omega'), with the last birth on 19 October 1995, and sets its story in January 2021 — the adaptation keeps the roughly eighteen-year gap but shifts both forward and swaps male infertility for female.

ending.why: One child is born and one boat is met at sea; whether the Human Project exists, or the species recovers, is never shown.

events.title: P. D. James publishes The Children of Men
events.description: James imagines England in 2021, twenty-six years after the last human birth, ruled by a self-appointed Warden and quietly organising its own extinction.
events.note: The novel's own dates are 1995 for the onset of infertility and January 2021 (its first diary entry is headed Friday 1 January 2021) for the story.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Year Omega (novel continuity)
events.description: In the novel the human race stops reproducing: all human sperm, even frozen, loses potency, and the last child is born — Joseph Ricardo, who is killed in a Buenos Aires pub brawl at twenty-five as the novel opens.
events.note: Novel continuity only, and male infertility rather than the film's female infertility; the film moves the same event to 2009 and the last child is Baby Diego. James calls 1995 'Year Omega'.
events.binWhy: Every human loses the ability to reproduce.

facets.change: fertile → no births anywhere

events.title: Cuaron's film released
events.description: The adaptation keeps the infertility but moves the story to a Britain of internment camps and barricades, pushing the crisis into the audience's own recent past rather than the year of filming.
events.note: Released in 2006 and set twenty-one years later, in 2027.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The last children are born
events.description: Humanity becomes infertile; the cohort born in 2009 is the last, and the youngest of them — Baby Diego — is stabbed to death in Buenos Aires at eighteen as the film opens.
events.note: Inferred from the film's 'eighteen years of infertility' and Baby Diego's age of eighteen years and four months, which puts his birth in mid-2009; the novel's equivalent is the male infertility of 1995, so the year is contested across adaptations — but real 2009 delivered no such thing, which is the point of plotting it.
events.binWhy: A disease or biological failure strikes on a mass scale.

facets.change: fertile → the last children born

events.title: Julian's baby (novel ending)
events.description: In the novel's present the dissident Julian gives birth to a boy, the first human birth in twenty-six years, and Theo Faron kills the Warden and takes his ring.
events.note: Novel continuity: the diary opens in January 2021 and the infertility dates from 1995. The film's equivalent birth happens in 2027 and is a girl, Kee's daughter.
events.binWhy: A child is born or a person chosen on whom the future turns.

facets.change: twenty-six years without → a birth; the ruler killed

events.title: Kee's baby, and the ship Tomorrow
events.description: In a Britain of refugee cages and closing borders, Kee gives birth to the first child in eighteen years and Theo gets her onto the fog-bound boat Tomorrow to reach the Human Project in the Azores.
events.note: The film never displays the year, but its own poster announces 'The year 2027: the last days of the human race. No child has been born for 18 years', and the opening news copy calls Diego's death a reminder of 'the 18 years of infertility'. Real 2027 is close, and no such crisis has happened.
events.binWhy: A child is born or a person chosen on whom the future turns.

facets.change: eighteen years without → a birth, and a boat out

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the branch is opened by one biological event inside living memory — the species simply stops conceiving in 2009 — and everything else in the film, from the siege of Seattle to the camps at Bexhill, is ordinary twenty-first-century politics reacting to it. Tier coverage is deliberately narrow and honest: T3 holds the two source works and the novel's 1995 onset; T2 holds the film's 2009 fork, the novel's 2021 ending and the film's 2027 present; T4 is empty because nothing in the story reaches back before living memory, and T1 is empty because the fiction simply stops — the last image is a boat vanishing into fog, and no adaptation, sequel or tie-in carries it beyond 2027. Its own arithmetic (a final cohort born in 2009, or 1995 in the novel) implies extinction in the 2060s-2080s if the Human Project fails, but no source dates that.

lineages.title: Interstellar
lineages.creator: Christopher Nolan

divergence.label: The wormhole near Saturn
divergence.delta: Real: 2019 is the year LIGO's catalogue fills with black-hole mergers and a Chinese lander touches down on the far side of the Moon. Fiction: something opens a traversable wormhole near Saturn, and by 2067 it is the only way off a starving Earth.
divergence.note: Nothing is dated on screen: the film says only that the wormhole 'appeared 48 years ago'. The year 2019 comes from Kip Thorne's tie-in book The Science of Interstellar, which Thorne introduces as his own extrapolation rather than Nolan's; chaining 2019 + 48 gives the standard 2067 present. The whole dating of this lineage is arithmetic from a tie-in reference, and the 13-year gap between the black-hole fall and Cooper's recovery is unexplained by any source.

ending.why: The equation is solved from inside the tesseract, Earth is evacuated, and a new world waits at the end of the wormhole.

events.title: Apollo 11, and the history the film rewrites
events.description: The Moon landings happen; two generations later the film's schools teach that they were faked to bankrupt the Soviets, a measure of how far the blight era has rewritten its own past.
events.note: The landing is real history; the classroom revisionism is canon dialogue in the film, undated there but implied to be a product of the crisis decades.
events.binWhy: The state teaches that the Moon landings were faked.

facets.change: the landings → officially declared a hoax

events.title: Interstellar released
events.description: Nolan's film arrives with Kip Thorne's gravitational physics attached, placing a wormhole 53 years into its own future and a blight only twenty years out.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The wormhole is found
events.description: An anomaly near Saturn turns out to be an artificial traversable wormhole; NASA's Lazarus missions follow it, and it becomes humanity's only route off Earth.
events.note: From the film's line that the wormhole appeared '48 years ago' relative to its 2067 present; the 2019 anchor itself is Kip Thorne's own extrapolation in the tie-in book, not something Nolan put on screen. The real 2019 produced gravitational-wave catalogues and no wormhole — the branch's fork is already behind us.
events.binWhy: A passage to somewhere unreachable is found or made.

facets.change: a dying world → a way off it appears near Saturn

events.title: The blight
events.description: A global crop blight begins destroying wheat, okra and finally everything but corn, collapsing food systems, triggering the Resource Wars and shrinking the human population.
events.note: No year is spoken on screen; the onset in the 2030s is a reconstruction. The film supplies only relative escalation — by its 2067 present wheat has been gone 'seven years', okra that same year, and corn is all that is left.
events.binWhy: A blight destroys the food supply crop by crop.

facets.change: harvests → destroyed crop by crop

events.title: The Lazarus missions
events.description: With the Resource Wars over and NASA reduced to a hidden bunker, twelve one-way probes are sent through the wormhole; three worlds answer — Miller's water world, Mann's ice world and Edmunds' desert world.
events.note: Reconstructed from the film's on-screen statement that the Lazarus missions left ten years before its present; the twelve astronauts are led by Dr Mann, and only Miller, Mann and Edmunds are named.
events.binWhy: A first mission leaves for territory nobody has reached.

facets.change: no way out → twelve one-way probes sent through

events.title: Cooper leaves on Endurance
events.description: Dust storms and a failing harvest frame the film's present: Cooper joins NASA's last mission and the Endurance departs for Saturn and the wormhole while Murph stays behind with the gravity equation.
events.note: Derived, not stated: 2019 plus the on-screen '48 years'. The film displays no year, and the day-level dates circulating online are fan reconstruction, so only the year is given here.
events.binWhy: A first mission leaves for territory nobody has reached.

facets.change: a failing harvest → the last mission leaves

events.title: Miller's planet: three hours, twenty-three years
events.description: One hour on the water world costs seven years outside it, so the landing party loses twenty-three years, Doyle, and any chance of catching the dead astronaut's signal.
events.note: Dated from the on-screen two-year transit to Saturn (2067-69) plus the stated dilation; the film gives the loss as twenty-three years, four months and eight days.
events.binWhy: The voyage costs twenty-three years in three hours.

facets.change: three hours → twenty-three years lost

events.title: Twenty-three years later: the return to Endurance
events.description: Cooper and Brand come back to a ship where twenty-three years passed in three hours: Murph is an adult, Professor Brand is dead, and the mission moves on to Mann's planet, where Mann tries to kill Cooper and dies in orbit.
events.note: Derived from the on-screen 'twenty-three years, four months, eight days'; the same figure is why Murph's generation has grown up while Cooper has not aged.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: the ship → reached after twenty-three years; a betrayal

events.title: Gargantua, and the tesseract
events.description: The slingshot around Gargantua costs fifty-one years; out of fuel, Cooper and TARS fall past the horizon into a tesseract built by future humans, where time is a physical dimension, and Cooper reaches back through Murph's bookshelf to hand her the quantum data that solves the gravity equation.
events.note: Derived from the on-screen line that the manoeuvre 'will cost us 51 years' (2092 + 51). The tesseract's builders are outside time, so the scene's own dating is necessarily Cooper's, not theirs.
events.binWhy: He reaches back through time to his daughter.

facets.change: past the horizon → a message sent back through time

events.title: Cooper wakes, 124 years old
events.description: Recovered near Saturn, Cooper wakes aboard Cooper Station, an O'Neill cylinder built with the equation Murph solved, finds his daughter an old woman on her deathbed, and steals a Ranger to go and find Brand.
events.note: Derived from the on-screen 'you are 124 years old'; a 13-year gap between the 2143 fall and this recovery is unexplained by the film, and the final montage of Brand alone on Edmunds' planet is undated.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: a dying Earth → humanity living in orbit

events.title: The bulk
events.description: Humanity's descendants have become five-dimensional beings for whom time is a navigable dimension, and by the film's own bootstrap logic they are the ones who opened the wormhole in 2019 and built the tesseract inside Gargantua.
events.note: Flagged deliberately: the film says only that they are us, 'a civilization that's evolved past the four dimensions', and never dates them, so 2500 is a marker for the branch's deep-time reach rather than a canon figure. If a strict no-invention reading is preferred, this is the one event to drop, leaving T1 empty.
events.binWhy: Humanity's descendants are five-dimensional beings.

facets.change: humans → five-dimensional descendants who reached back

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the film's fork is a single object — a wormhole that appears near Saturn in what is now our recent past — dropped into a recognisable, failing twenty-first-century Earth; the blight is slow climate catastrophe, not space opera, and everything after it is arithmetic on that one event. Tiers: nothing in the fiction reaches back before the Apollo era, so T4 is empty; T3 holds only 1969 and the film's own rewriting of it; T2 runs from the film's 2014 release through the blight, the Lazarus missions, the Endurance, the twenty-three lost years, the fifty-one-year slingshot and the 2156 Cooper Station epilogue; T1 holds one deliberately flagged marker for the undated fifth-dimensional 'bulk'. The film's final images — Brand alone on Edmunds' planet, the Plan B colony — are never dated, and the colony dates circulating online are fan reconstruction, so no event is given for them.

lineages.title: The Expanse
lineages.creator: James S. A. Corey (Daniel Abraham & Ty Franck)

divergence.label: The first permanent settlement on Mars
divergence.delta: Real: no human has walked on Mars, no permanent settlement there is on any agency's schedule, and the Moon has only temporary visitors. Fiction: a permanent Martian colony is founded in 2050, and within two centuries Mars is terraformed, sovereign, and fielding its own navy against Earth.
divergence.note: The year comes from the TV series' production design guide (the books say only 'colonised in the 21st century'); the same source puts a permanent lunar colony in 2025. The invention everyone remembers, the Epstein Drive, comes later, in 2213-14, and is what opens the Belt — but the Mars settlement is the first fork.

ending.why: Humanity survives the ring gates, the empire and the things that ate the gate-builders; a thousand years on it is still here and still plural.

events.title: The ring builders seed Phoebe
events.description: A galaxy-spanning civilisation parks a protomolecule payload inside an interstellar asteroid aimed at the primitive Earth, which Saturn captures and which becomes the moon Phoebe.
events.note: Canon states roughly two billion years; this is the deep backstory that the whole branch eventually detonates, and the only pre-modern material the series has.
events.binWhy: An alien civilisation touches the primitive Earth without anyone knowing.

facets.change: an empty system → seeded by a civilisation long gone

events.title: Leviathan Wakes published
events.description: The first Expanse novel appears, set in a solar system that is what ours becomes if fusion travel arrives: an overpopulated Earth, a terraforming Mars, and a Belt that does the work and gets none of the gravity.
events.note: The series grew out of the authors' tabletop setting, which was literally named '2350' — the origin of the series-present date used here.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The first permanent lunar colony
events.description: In the fiction the Moon is permanently settled in 2025, becoming the shipyard and launch pad for everything that follows.
events.note: Design-guide date (the RPG says only 'the 2000s'). Real 2025 passed with robotic landers and the Artemis Accords and no permanent base — the branch's first missed milestone, and the reason this lineage is plottable against our own decade.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: visits → the Moon permanently settled

events.title: The first permanent settlement on Mars
events.description: Humanity's first permanent settlement on another planet is founded, beginning both the Martian project of making a dead world live and the long resentment of the world that claims to own it.
events.note: Design-guide date; the novels give no year, only 'the 21st century' and 'about three generations' before the Epstein Drive.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: one world → the first settlement on another

events.title: Eros becomes a deep-system base
events.description: The Mars-crossing asteroid Eros is occupied and used as a staging base for exploration of the outer system, the first foothold beyond the inner planets.
events.note: Design-guide date; the same asteroid is later the site of the protomolecule catastrophe, which gives the early colonisation its retrospective weight.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: inner planets → a foothold in the outer system

events.title: Mars starts rejecting Earth rule
events.description: A century after the first colony, Martian society begins openly refusing United Nations authority, and the Earth-Mars cold war that frames the series takes shape.
events.note: Design-guide date; canon stresses that the split is generational rather than a single act, and the formal independence demand follows around 2200-2213.
events.binWhy: A colony begins refusing the homeworld's authority; a cold war forms.

facets.change: a colony → openly refusing the homeworld's authority

events.title: The Epstein Drive, and Martian independence
events.description: Solomon Epstein's modified fusion drive makes continuous-thrust travel possible and turns the Belt and outer moons into places people can live; Mars trades the drive to Earth for sovereignty and the Martian Congressional Republic is proclaimed the same year.
events.note: Contested: on screen the drive is dated 137 years before the series' 2350s present (2213-14), the wiki's prose rounds it to c. 2213, and the TV design guide says 2200. The independence trade is dated to the same year in the wiki's reconstruction.
events.binWhy: A new capability is switched on.

facets.change: slow travel → continuous thrust; independence bought with it

events.title: The Belt fills up
events.description: The drive triggers a gold rush: hundreds of settlements, stations and ships across the Belt, Ceres as its port city, and functioning settlements on the major moons of Jupiter and Saturn.
events.note: Reconstructed from the wiki's era table; the novels describe the Belt's settlement in detail but never date it.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: empty rock → hundreds of settlements

events.title: The Vesta Blockade
events.description: A UN blockade over Martian terraforming supplies becomes the closest thing yet to open war: one MCRN cruiser cripples five UNN destroyers, and half the UN fleet burns for Mars before cooler heads prevail.
events.note: TV continuity: Avasarala dates it 'forty years' before the series' 2350s present.
events.binWhy: A blockade brings the two powers to the edge of war and no further.

facets.change: cold war → a blockade brings the fleets to the edge

events.title: The Anderson Station massacre
events.description: UN forces storm a Belt station over a water protest and kill the people inside; the officer who gave the order, Fred Johnson, defects to the Belt and becomes the face of the Outer Planets Alliance.
events.note: The novels place it four years before the 2340 Pallas revolt, which is a decade before Leviathan Wakes, so c. 2336; the TV continuity's table gives 2339.
events.binWhy: State forces kill protesters over water; the massacre creates the opposition.

facets.change: a protest → the state kills everyone inside

events.title: The alien substance on Phoebe
events.description: A Martian survey of the moon Phoebe recovers something that is not geology; Mars brings in the Protogen corporation to study it in secret, and the protomolecule enters human history.
events.note: Design-guide/wiki dating (the books' relative era 0-1 XTE corresponds to c. 2342-43); the Mars-Protogen base on Phoebe follows in 2345.
events.binWhy: A non-human intelligence is confirmed, met or intervenes.

facets.change: geology → something alien, studied in secret

events.title: Leviathan Wakes: the Canterbury and Eros
events.description: The series opens with the ice hauler Canterbury destroyed and Julie Mao dying of protomolecule exposure on Eros; the Mormon generation ship Nauvoo is hijacked and thrown at the station, and its hundred thousand people are driven into Venus.
events.note: The series never prints a year: 2350 comes from the authors' original RPG (named 2350), the wiki's reconstruction and ScreenRant's timeline; the official RPG map is marked 2351 because it is set in the gap between books one and two.
events.binWhy: A ship is destroyed and a hundred thousand people are killed on a station.

facets.change: cold war → a ship destroyed, a station's people fed to an experiment

events.title: The ring gate opens
events.description: The protomolecule's growth on Venus becomes a vast ring beyond Uranus; when a Belter slingshotter flies through it the gate activates and more than thirteen hundred habitable systems open at once.
events.note: TV dating (ring forms 2352, fleet arrives 2353, '187 days later'); the books' Abaddon's Gate corresponds to c. 2354, so the books run a year or two later than the show.
events.binWhy: A passage to somewhere unreachable is found or made.

facets.change: one system → thirteen hundred open at once

events.title: The bombardment of Earth
events.description: Marco Inaros's Free Navy throws stealth-coated asteroids at Earth, killing millions and dusting the sky, while the colony systems beyond the gates begin to break away from the inner planets.
events.note: TV: the strikes fall in 2355 and the Free Navy war ends in late 2356; the novels' Nemesis Games and Babylon's Ashes cover the same ground c. 2359-60.
events.binWhy: An attack or disaster kills on a scale that remakes society.

facets.change: the homeworld → struck by asteroids; the colonies break away

events.title: Laconia takes the gate network
events.description: Thirty years after the Free Navy war, the renegade Martian fleet that vanished through a gate returns as the Laconian Empire and seizes the slow zone with ring-builder technology.
events.note: Persepolis Rising jumps 'thirty years' past Babylon's Ashes; the wiki's reconstruction lands c. 2390, with Tiamat's Wrath c. 2393-94 and Leviathan Falls c. 2395.
events.binWhy: A returned fleet seizes the gate network by force.

facets.change: a vanished fleet → returns as an empire and seizes the network

events.title: The gates close
events.description: The war against Laconia ends with the ring network destroyed, stranding all thirteen hundred colony systems from one another and from Earth.
events.note: Leviathan Falls (2021); the year is reconstructed from the wiki's relative chronology, not printed in the novel.
events.binWhy: The order of society breaks and does not come back.

facets.change: an empire → defeated by destroying the network itself

events.title: A thousand years later: the Thirty Worlds reach Earth
events.description: In the epilogue humanity has built its own faster-than-light drive; a delegation from the Thirty Worlds crosses to a depopulated Earth and is met by Amos Burton, still alive.
events.note: Wikipedia's plot summary states the epilogue is set a thousand years after Leviathan Falls and that the gate collapse stranded 1,300 colony systems; the novel prints no year, so c. 3395 is arithmetic from the reconstruction above.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: stranded colonies → return to a depopulated homeworld

lineages.groupingNote: The cleanest case in this group: no aliens arrive and no history is rewritten — this is what our own solar system becomes if one propulsion breakthrough lands, so the branch is drawn entirely in the fiction's own future. Tiers: T4 holds only the ring builders' two-billion-year-old payload; there is no T3 material, because the branch's history only starts in the twenty-first century; T2 carries the lunar and Martian settlements, the Epstein Drive and the Belt gold rush; T1 carries the whole series present, the ring gate, the Free Navy war, the Laconian conquest and the millennium after the gates close.

lineages.title: The Handmaid's Tale
lineages.creator: Margaret Atwood

divergence.label: The President's Day Massacre
divergence.delta: Real: February 1999 — the Senate acquits Bill Clinton at his impeachment trial on 12 February, three days before Presidents' Day, and the constitutional crisis ends with Congress and the presidency intact. Fiction: the President is shot and Congress machine-gunned, the army declares a state of emergency, the attack is blamed on Islamic fanatics, and the Constitution is suspended as a temporary measure that never ends.
divergence.inUniverse: The President's Day Massacre (named in the Historical Notes, which suspect Commander B. Frederick Judd of orchestrating it); no year is ever stated
divergence.note: Neither novel gives a year, so it is derived. (1) The Historical Notes cite a paper titled 'Iran and Gilead: Two Late-Twentieth-Century Monotheocracies', so Gilead begins before 2001. (2) Offred is 33 in her narrative; her daughter was three or four when women's accounts were frozen, a few weeks after the attack, five when the family was caught at the border, and is eight in the narrative, so the narrative falls about four years after the coup. (3) Offred recalls riots over pornography and abortion, with clinics being bombed, when she was fourteen or fifteen; read against the real wave of clinic bombings in 1984, she was born about 1970, which puts her narrative about 2003 and the coup about 1999. (4) This agrees with Joyce Carol Oates's 2006 reading that the narrative is set around 2005, and with The Testaments, where Lydia is 53 at the takeover and in her early seventies at the climax and Offred about fifty. 1999 is the latest year that keeps Gilead plainly late-twentieth-century; anything from the mid-1990s to 2000 fits the text. The name places the attack in February. The fork is put at the coup rather than at the earlier fertility collapse because the collapse is never dated and blends into real 1980s anxieties. The Hulu series dates the attack to September 2014; that is a different continuity.

ending.why: The leaked files bring on a purge, a military coup and a popular revolt that end Gilead and restore the United States, and by 2197 the regime is a subject for historians while Becka's statue is dedicated by the sisters, their mother and their grandchildren.

events.title: The Handmaid's Tale is published
events.description: Margaret Atwood publishes the novel she began in West Berlin in 1984: a Handmaid's account of the first years of a theocracy that has replaced the United States, closed by a scholarly epilogue set in 2195.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Handmaid's Tale

events.note: Published by McClelland & Stewart in Canada in 1985; winner of the Governor General's Award that year and of the first Arthur C. Clarke Award in 1987. Written after Reagan's election, with the Iranian revolution as a stated model.
events.binWhy: A publication, not an event in the story's world, so it takes no bin.

events.title: The birth rate collapses
events.description: Stillbirths, miscarriages and deformities rise and the birth rate falls steeply, which the Historical Notes blame on pollution, pesticides, nuclear accidents, leaks from chemical and biological weapons stockpiles, a strain of syphilis, AIDS and birth control. Men who will become the Sons of Jacob organise think tanks around the falling white birth rate, the grievance the coup will exploit.
events.inUniverse: The pre-Gilead decline in births; the Sons of Jacob Think Tanks (Historical Notes)

sources.title: LitCharts: Historical Notes on The Handmaid's Tale (causes of infertility; the Sons of Jacob)
BookRags: Notes on the Historical Notes (pollution, birth control, declining Caucasian birth rate)
Encyclopedia.com: The Handmaid's Tale (waste and war leave most women sterile)

events.note: Undated in both novels: the Historical Notes describe a late-twentieth-century decline, and the think tanks formed after a superpower arms stalemate and a classified Spheres of Influence Accord. The year is a marker, not a stated date: it is the approximate birth year of Offred's daughter (about four at the 1999 coup), placing the event inside the decade before the coup. Several of the causes it names (AIDS, pesticides, nuclear accidents) are real 1980s fears; the fiction's step is that together they sterilise most of a population. The novels describe no market crash, so no economic event is included.
events.binWhy: A biological failure sterilises a society on a mass scale and gives the coup its pretext.

facets.change: falling births → a society that cannot replace itself

events.title: The President's Day Massacre and the suspension of the Constitution
events.description: The Sons of Jacob shoot the President and machine-gun Congress, blame Islamic fanatics, and have the army declare a state of emergency and suspend the Constitution. Weeks later, on one day, every woman's account is frozen and passed to her nearest male relative and women are dismissed from their jobs; women who march are fired on, and women professionals are rounded up into a stadium.
events.inUniverse: The President's Day Massacre (Historical Notes); the aftermath is Offred's chapter 28 and Lydia's arrest in The Testaments

sources.title: Crossref-it: The Handmaid's Tale, chapter 28
Novelguide: The Handmaid's Tale, chapters 25-28 (Compunumbers wiped, women dismissed)
The Handmaid's Tale Wiki (Fandom): President's Day Massacre
The Handmaid's Tale Wiki (Fandom): Aunt Lydia (novel), arrested as the credit cards are cancelled

events.note: Year derived as set out in the divergence note; February follows from the name. Offred says things stayed in suspended animation for weeks, with newspapers censored, roadblocks and Identipasses, before the day women lost their money and work, so the freeze belongs to the same year and is merged here. The Testaments has Lydia's office raided the day the cards are cancelled. What made the freeze possible was a cashless Compubank economy already in place.
events.binWhy: A faction massacres the government, blames an outside enemy and takes the state; the attack is the instrument, the seizure is the event.

facets.change: a constitutional republic → emergency rule by the Sons of Jacob

events.title: Gilead founds the Handmaid system
events.description: The new republic voids second marriages, declares the wives in them adulteresses and takes their children. Fertile women are trained by the Aunts at the Rachel and Leah Centre and assigned to Commanders' households to bear children for them. Offred, caught at the Canadian border with her husband and five-year-old daughter, is among the first wave.
events.inUniverse: Offred is 'among the first wave of women recruited for reproductive purposes' (Historical Notes)

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Handmaid's Tale (the capture, the voided divorce, the daughter taken)
Wikipedia: The Testaments (Lydia chosen by Commander Judd to found the Aunts)

events.note: Derived: Offred's daughter was three or four at the 1999 freeze and five at the capture, so the capture and the Red Center fall about a year after the coup. The Aunts themselves were founded by Lydia and a few others picked out of the stadium by Commander Judd in the months after the attack. The Historical Notes say Gilead's forms were borrowed from other societies, and name Commander Frederick Waterford as the probable designer of the Handmaids' red dress.
events.binWhy: The regime creates the institution the whole world is known by: a caste of conscripted child-bearers and the women who train them.

facets.change: free women → state-assigned Handmaids

events.title: Offred's story
events.description: On her third posting, with Commander Fred in Cambridge, Offred is drawn into the Commander's forbidden evenings, a sanctioned affair with the driver Nick, and the Mayday resistance, whose password her shopping partner Ofglen gives her. Ofglen hangs herself when the Eyes come; at the end men in a black van take Offred away, and Nick tells her it is Mayday.
events.inUniverse: The narrative present of The Handmaid's Tale, spring to summer

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Handmaid's Tale
The Handmaid's Tale Wiki (Fandom): Offred (novel), aged 33
The Handmaid's Tale Wiki (Fandom): Mayday

events.note: Derived: Offred is 33 and her daughter, five at the capture, 'must be' eight, about four years after the 1999 coup. Joyce Carol Oates put it at about 2005. The Historical Notes say the tapes were found in a U.S. Army footlocker in Bangor, Maine, on the Underground Femaleroad, which suggests she got out, and that Waterford was purged soon after. In our 2003 the United States invaded Iraq; the fiction's United States is closed, and its resistance runs on passwords and vans.
events.binWhy: An ordinary woman is drawn into the hidden resistance and the Commander's secret life; the story is her call.

facets.change: a compliant Handmaid → a woman in Mayday's hands

events.title: Baby Nicole is smuggled into Canada
events.description: The Handmaid conceives a daughter in her Commander's household, goes underground with the newborn and hands her to Mayday near the border to be carried into Canada. Gilead calls it kidnapping and demands her back for the next sixteen years; Canada's protesters put her face on their posters.
events.inUniverse: 'Baby Nicole', later raised in Toronto as Daisy (The Testaments)

sources.title: The Handmaid's Tale Wiki (Fandom): Daisy (novel)

The Testaments' epilogue only suggests that the mother is Offred; the atlas follows that reading and says so.

events.title: The Testaments is published
events.description: Atwood publishes the sequel, told by Aunt Lydia and two young women, one raised in Gilead and one in Toronto, and closed by a second symposium in 2197. It shares the 2019 Booker Prize.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Testaments

events.description: Aunt Lydia, secretly Mayday's mole, has spent years collecting evidence of the Commanders' crimes. Nicole, sent into Gilead after her adoptive parents are murdered on her sixteenth birthday, escapes by sea with her half-sister Agnes carrying the files on a microdot in a tattoo, and the Canadian media publish them.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Testaments
The Handmaid's Tale Wiki (Fandom): Daisy (novel)

facets.change: crimes buried in Ardua Hall → published in Canada

events.title: Purge, military coup and the fall of Gilead
events.description: The leaks set off a purge of the elite, which provokes a military coup and a popular revolt. Gilead is weakened and falls, and the United States is restored by Mayday and the American holdouts.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Testaments (the purge, the coup, the fall and restoration)

events.title: The Twelfth Symposium on Gileadean Studies
events.description: At the University of Denay, Nunavit, Professor Pieixoto of Cambridge presents the transcribed cassettes found in a footlocker in Bangor, Maine, as 'The Handmaid's Tale'. Gilead is a period for academic study, with scarce records because its Great Purge destroyed them, and the scholars joke about the material.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com: The Handmaid's Tale (symposium held on 25 June 2195)
LitCharts: Historical Notes on The Handmaid's Tale

events.note: The only date either novel states outright. The epilogue shows an Arctic Canada with Indigenous names, a woman chairing the session and a male scholar condescending to his source; Atwood's point is that the regime is gone but its attitudes survive in how its history is told.

facets.change: a living regime → an academic field

events.title: The Thirteenth Symposium on Gileadean Studies
events.description: Pieixoto presents two newer finds: Aunt Lydia's manuscript, hidden inside a copy of Newman's Apologia Pro Vita Sua, and the witness testimonies of Agnes and Nicole. He suggests their mother was Offred, and describes a statue of Becka put up by the sisters with their mother, both fathers, their children and grandchildren.
events.inUniverse: The Thirteenth Symposium, the epilogue of The Testaments

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Testaments (Thirteenth Symposium, 2197)
The Handmaid's Tale Wiki (Fandom): The Thirteenth Symposium

events.binWhy: A second jump forward shows what became of the women who brought Gilead down.

facets.change: hidden testimonies → the documented fall of Gilead

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because it leaves our history by one political event inside a recognisably real United States, a decade and a half after the book was written, and walks forward from there in our calendar. It follows the novels' continuity (The Handmaid's Tale, 1985, and The Testaments, 2019, including both epilogues); the Hulu series (2017-2025), which dates the attack to 2014, names Offred June and invents much of the middle, is not followed. Tiers covered are T3 (1985-1999) and T2 (2000-2197). T4 is empty because the fiction reaches back only to Offred's childhood, and T1 is empty because the last glimpse is the 2197 symposium.
