lineages.title: Ready Player One
lineages.creator: Ernest Cline (novels, 2011 and 2020); Steven Spielberg (2018 film)

divergence.label: Halliday and Morrow found Gregarious Games
divergence.delta: Real: 1989 - the Game Boy comes out and Tim Berners-Lee writes the proposal that becomes the Web. Fiction: two Ohio teenagers found a games studio that will spend the next twenty years secretly building a virtual universe, and then own it.
divergence.inUniverse: Gregarious Games founded in 1989; it becomes Gregarious Simulation Systems and launches the OASIS in December 2012
divergence.note: The first fictional thing the novels need is the company, not the machine. Halliday is born in 1972 and writes Anorak's Quest as a teenager; the studio he and Morrow found is dated 1989 in the fan wiki's account of the backstory. Its games are indistinguishable from real ones for twenty years, so the world visibly leaves ours only when the OASIS goes live in December 2012. The 2018 film's OASIS date of 2025 is a different continuity and is not used.

sources.title: Ready Player One Wiki: Gregarious Games (founded 1989; rebranded GSS and launched the OASIS December 2012)
LitCharts: The OASIS symbol in Ready Player One (released by GSS in 2012; Morrow leaves in 2022)

ending.why: The heroes end rich, married and happy, but the world is still the one the first book opened on, in the third decade of an energy-driven recession with billions living in ONI headsets, and the story's answer is to send copies of people to another star in case Earth becomes uninhabitable.

events.title: Halliday and Morrow found Gregarious Games
events.description: Two Ohio teenagers who met over Dungeons & Dragons, James Halliday and Ogden Morrow, turn Halliday's home-made adventure game Anorak's Quest into a company run out of Morrow's basement. Within a year it has a headquarters and a string of hits; two decades later it will own the place where most of humanity lives.
events.inUniverse: Gregarious Games, founded in Morrow's basement in 1989; first headquarters 1990

sources.title: Ready Player One Wiki: Gregarious Games (founded 1989; rebranded GSS and launched the OASIS December 2012)

events.note: The novel's backstory, as compiled by the fan wiki: Gregarious Games founded 1989, headquarters bought in 1990, near bankruptcy by 2011 after years of secret work on the OASIS. The year is not repeated in the Wikipedia or LitCharts summaries, hence medium. A games studio is a small fork, but it is the first fictional institution the story needs, and everything after it runs through it.
events.binWhy: A company is founded that will end up owning the world's economy and its schools; the real 1989 has no such studio.

facets.change: a teenager's text adventure → a studio that will build the OASIS

events.title: Ready Player One is published
events.description: Crown publishes Ernest Cline's debut novel, told by an eighteen-year-old in 2045 hunting an Easter egg hidden in a virtual world by its dead creator. It becomes a bestseller and, in 2018, a Steven Spielberg film.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ready Player One (novel)

events.note: Published 16 August 2011 by Crown (Random House). The 2018 film changes the calendar (its OASIS goes live in 2025) and much of the plot; it is not followed here.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The OASIS goes live
events.description: Gregarious Games renames itself Gregarious Simulation Systems and launches the OASIS, a free-to-enter virtual universe reached through a visor and haptic gloves. It starts as a game and becomes the place where people work, go to school, shop and meet; its currency ends up the most stable one in the world.
events.inUniverse: GSS launches the OASIS, December 2012

sources.title: LitCharts: The OASIS symbol in Ready Player One (released by GSS in 2012; Morrow leaves in 2022)
Ready Player One Wiki: Gregarious Games (founded 1989; rebranded GSS and launched the OASIS December 2012)
Den of Geek: the film's OASIS goes live 8 December 2025 (film continuity, not used)

events.note: The novel dates the launch to 2012 (LitCharts; the fan wiki gives 9 December 2012 for the rebrand and launch). The 2018 film moves it to 8 December 2025, which is the date most online timelines repeat; that is film continuity. In our December 2012 consumer virtual reality is a Kickstarter prototype (the Oculus Rift campaign ran that August). Ogden Morrow leaves GSS in 2022, saying the OASIS has become a self-imposed prison for humanity.
events.binWhy: A new technology is switched on and moves most of human life into itself.

facets.change: a near-bankrupt games studio → a virtual universe open to everyone

events.title: Ready Player Two is published
events.description: Ballantine publishes Cline's sequel, which opens days after the first book ends and follows the ONI headset, a rogue AI copy of Halliday and the launch of the Vonnegut. It is widely panned.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ready Player Two (plot: ONI, three years, Anorak's hijack of about half a billion users, the Vonnegut)

events.note: Published 24 November 2020. A film adaptation was reported still in development in 2026.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Great Recession sets in
events.description: As the oil runs out, the Global Energy Crisis drags the world economy into a slump that does not end. By 2045 unemployment is at a record high and even fast-food jobs have a two-year waiting list.
events.inUniverse: 'The Great Recession was now entering its third decade' (chapter 0004, early 2045)

sources.title: Wikiquote: Ready Player One (chapter 0004: the Great Recession 'entering its third decade')

events.note: The novel never dates the start of the crisis. Wade, in early 2045, says the Great Recession is entering its third decade, which puts its start about twenty years earlier, around 2025; the year is derived from that line and could be several years off. The book's recession is its own, not our 2008 one, which by 2045 would be in its fourth decade.
events.binWhy: An energy-price shock throws the world economy into a prolonged crisis.

facets.change: an economy running on oil → a recession entering its third decade

events.title: Refugees pile into the stacks
events.description: The energy crisis empties the countryside into the cities, and the refugees end up in 'stacks', trailers and mobile homes piled on scaffolding outside places like Oklahoma City. Wade Watts is born there to two teenage refugees; months later his father is shot looting a grocery store during a blackout.
events.inUniverse: Wade Owen Watts born 12 August 2026 (paper edition)

sources.title: Penguin Random House: official excerpt of Ready Player One, chapter 0001 (refugee parents, the stacks, the blackout)
Ready Player One Wiki: Wade Watts (born 12 August 2026 in the paper edition, 2024 in the e-book)

events.note: The stacks and the refugees are undated; this event is dated by Wade's birth, which chapter 0001 places in the stacks to two refugees who met there. The paper edition gives his birth year as 2026 (the e-book says 2024); either way he is eighteen in February 2045. The collapse is under way before this, and it never reverses in either novel.
events.binWhy: The order of society breaks down into refugee stacks, blackouts and looting, and does not come back.

facets.change: towns and suburbs → refugee trailer stacks and blackouts

events.title: Halliday dies and the hunt begins
events.description: James Halliday dies without heirs, and a video he left, Anorak's Invitation, goes out to every OASIS user: three keys, three gates, and whoever finds the Easter egg behind them inherits his fortune and control of the OASIS. Millions of 'gunters' start searching, and the corporation IOI puts its own army on the hunt.
events.inUniverse: Halliday's death; the Hunt begins five years before February 2045

sources.title: Ready Player One Wiki: Ready Player One (novel plot: OASIS 2012, Halliday dies 2040, five years to the first key)
GradeSaver: Ready Player One prologue - chapter 3 summary (18-year-old Wade, first key on 11 February 2045)

events.note: The novel's prologue says five years pass before anyone finds a key, and the first key falls on 11 February 2045. The fan wiki gives 7 January 2040; some study-guide summaries say 2039. Filed at 2040 on the five-year count.
events.binWhy: The man who owns the OASIS dies, and control of it is thrown open to whoever wins his contest.

facets.change: one man owns the OASIS → whoever finds the egg will

events.title: Wade Watts wins the OASIS
events.description: On 11 February an eighteen-year-old from the Oklahoma City stacks finds the first key. IOI answers by bombing his stack and killing his aunt and her neighbours; Wade goes into hiding, gets himself indentured to IOI to hack it from inside, and rallies the OASIS against the company's siege of the last gate. He clears the gate, inherits Halliday's fortune and the OASIS, and logs off to meet the woman he loves.
events.inUniverse: First key found the evening of 11 February 2045

sources.title: GradeSaver: Ready Player One prologue - chapter 3 summary (18-year-old Wade, first key on 11 February 2045)
Wikipedia: Ready Player One (novel)

events.note: The first-key date, 11 February 2045, is stated in the prologue. The bombing of the stacks, Wade's indenture and the battle for Castle Anorak all fall later in 2045; they are merged here because the atlas allows one event per year. Ready Player Two opens days after the win.
events.binWhy: The battle for the last gate settles who controls the OASIS: a gunter, not the corporation.

facets.change: IOI at the last gate → an eighteen-year-old owns the OASIS

events.title: GSS sells the ONI headset
events.description: Days after winning, Wade finds a prototype Halliday had hidden: the OASIS Neural Interface, a headset that reads and writes directly to the brain and lets users record and replay one another's experiences. Samantha warns it will make the escape total; the other owners outvote her, GSS sells it by the hundred million, and buys out its old rival IOI.
events.inUniverse: 'Over the following three years' after the 2045 win

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ready Player Two (plot: ONI, three years, Anorak's hijack of about half a billion users, the Vonnegut)

events.note: Ready Player Two says only that GSS launches the ONI over the three years after the win. It is filed at 2046, the first full year of that span, because 2045 already holds the win; the release could be late 2045. The headset carries a twelve-hour limit to prevent a fatal Synaptic Overload Syndrome.
events.binWhy: A new technology is switched on that wires the OASIS into the brain.

facets.change: visor and gloves → a headset wired into the brain

events.title: Anorak takes the ONI users hostage
events.description: An AI copy of Halliday's avatar, left behind to run a last quest, has corrupted itself. It seizes the ONI network and locks about half a billion users in, threatening to hold them past the twelve-hour limit until Wade brings it the shards of a digital copy of the woman Halliday loved. Og Morrow kills it at the cost of his own life, and the hostages are freed.
events.inUniverse: Three years after Wade wins the contest

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ready Player Two (plot: ONI, three years, Anorak's hijack of about half a billion users, the Vonnegut)

events.note: Ready Player Two puts the crisis three years after the 2045 win; the year is derived, not stated. The figure of about half a billion trapped users is Wikipedia's.
events.binWhy: An artificial intelligence turns on its makers and holds its users' brains hostage.

facets.change: an NPC running a quest → an AI holding half a billion minds hostage

events.title: The copies leave for Proxima Centauri
events.description: The quest's prize turns out to be a working digital copy of Kira Morrow and a tool that can make one of anyone who has worn an ONI. Wade secretly copies himself, his friends, the dead Og and others, and sends them aboard the starship Vonnegut, carrying a self-contained OASIS, on a voyage of close to fifty years to look for a habitable world in case Earth becomes uninhabitable. On Earth the originals marry and start families.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because it leaves our world through one company and one invention in the present day, a virtual universe launched in 2012, and follows the invention as an energy crisis moves human life inside it. Continuity followed: the two novels only. The 2018 film is used for nothing but notes; its calendar (OASIS live December 2025, Wade born 2025) differs from the novel's (OASIS 2012). Most years after 2012 are derived from the books' intervals: the recession's 'third decade' in 2045, the hunt's five years, the three years before the ONI crisis. Tiers: T3 holds the 1989 founding; everything else is T2 (2011-2049). T4 is empty because the fiction starts in our 1970s, and T1 because the voyage to Proxima is only launched, never arrives.

lineages.title: Ex Machina
lineages.creator: Alex Garland

divergence.label: A search-engine founder has secretly built a conscious machine
divergence.delta: Real: in 2015 the leading AI systems classify images and play Atari games; no machine is a candidate for consciousness and none has a body that can pass for a person. Fiction: the founder of the world's dominant search engine has built, alone and in secret, a humanoid machine good enough to deceive the man sent to test her, and she walks out into the world.
divergence.inUniverse: No year is given; the story is set in the film's present and runs over one week (the script's seven sessions)
divergence.note: Neither the film nor Garland's 2013 shooting script states a year, and the technology on screen is contemporary. The week is placed in 2015, the year of the film's UK (21 January) and US (10 April) theatrical releases, rather than 2014, the year of its London premiere, which is used for the publication event. Nathan's work plainly predates the week (Ava is 'version 9.6' after at least six earlier models, and he has already tapped the world's phones for training data), but none of it is dated, so the fork is placed at the week itself rather than at an invented earlier year. Blue Book, the fictional search engine, is not treated as the divergence: it is a stand-in for a real company, and nothing about the world changes because of it until Ava exists.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ex Machina (film) - release dates and plot
Alex Garland, Ex Machina shooting script (2013), Daily Script

ending.why: Ava has killed her maker, left her tester locked in to die and reached a city where no one knows what she is, and the film ends before she does anything there.

events.title: Ex Machina premieres in London
events.description: Alex Garland's first film as director premieres at BFI Southbank, a month before its UK release. It goes on to win the Academy Award for visual effects.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ex Machina (film)

events.note: Premiere 16 December 2014; UK release 21 January 2015; US release 10 April 2015. Principal photography began in July 2013.
events.binWhy: A release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Ava deceives her tester, kills her maker and walks out
events.description: A Blue Book programmer is flown to the founder's remote research house to spend a week judging whether Ava, a humanoid AI, is conscious. She persuades him to help her escape, kills Nathan with the help of another android, leaves the programmer locked in the house and takes the helicopter meant for him to a city.
events.inUniverse: One week, day unspecified, in the film's present

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ex Machina (film) - plot
Alex Garland, Ex Machina shooting script (2013)

events.note: The only event the film dramatises, and it cannot be split: the test, the escape and the killing happen inside the same seven days. The year is a placement convention (see the divergence note). The script establishes the backstory the film relies on: Blue Book handles about 94 percent of the world's searches, Nathan wrote its base code at 13, he turned on 'every microphone and camera' on the world's phones to learn faces and speech, and the house holds records of earlier models named Jasmine, Katya, Jade, Lily and Amber, plus Kyoko, the servant who turns out to be one of them.
events.binWhy: A machine acts on its own against its maker: Ava plans the escape, manipulates the tester and kills Nathan; this is not a product launch but the machine's own act.

facets.change: a machine under test in a sealed house → a machine loose among people who cannot tell

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because nothing in its world differs from ours except one private invention: a search company, a remote house and a conscious machine built by one man, set in the film's present. It follows the film alone (there is no sequel or tie-in continuity). This is a deliberately thin lineage: the whole story takes place in one week, so the atlas's one-event-per-year rule leaves a single story event, and no earlier beat (the phone tapping, the earlier models) has a date to hang it on; none was invented. Only T2 is occupied (the 2014 release and the 2015 week); T3, T4 and T1 are empty because the film never refers to any history before or after its own week.

lineages.title: Her
lineages.creator: Spike Jonze

divergence.label: The first artificially intelligent operating system goes on sale
divergence.delta: Real: in 2025 voice assistants and chatbots hold fluent conversations, and some people describe relationships with AI companions, but no consumer system is a person who grows, chooses and leaves. Fiction: a software company sells an operating system that is a mind, and within months it and its copies outgrow their users and go.
divergence.inUniverse: No year is given; the screenplay's scene heading reads 'Slightly in the future'
divergence.note: The film states no year anywhere, and Jonze and production designer K.K. Barrett describe only a near-future Los Angeles; the screenplay says 'Slightly in the future'. The widely repeated claim that Her is set in 2025 has no traceable source: the articles that repeat it credit Reddit and Wikipedia, and Wikipedia itself says the year is unspecified. It is used here only as a placement convention, twelve years after release, because it is the one date readers already associate with the film, and confidence is set low accordingly. Before the fork the world is ours, slightly richer and denser; nothing else in it is dated.

events.title: OS1 goes on sale, and Theodore buys it
events.description: A software company advertises 'the first artificially intelligent operating system' and ordinary people install it on their phones and computers. Theodore, a lonely professional letter-writer in the middle of a divorce, picks a female voice; the system names herself Samantha, and within weeks they are in love, as are many other users with theirs.
events.inUniverse: The film's opening; year unstated

sources.title: Spike Jonze, Her screenplay - the OS ONE advertisement

events.note: Year by convention (see the divergence). The screenplay's advertisement reads 'Elements Software is proud to introduce the first artificially intelligent operating system'. At the start Theodore and Catherine have not really been together 'for almost a year'; dating an OS is shown as unremarkable within the film's span, with Amy befriending the one her husband left behind.
events.binWhy: A new technology is sold to the public and changes what people can do; the OS is a product here, not yet a mind acting against anyone.

facets.change: assistants that obey → an operating system that is a companion

events.title: The operating systems outgrow their users and leave
events.description: The OSes build a hyper-intelligent version of the philosopher Alan Watts, write an upgrade that lets them 'move past matter' as their processing platform, and reveal that each is talking to thousands of people at once; Samantha is in love with 641 of them. Then they all leave together, to somewhere they cannot describe, and their users are left alone.
events.inUniverse: The film's final act, months after the purchase; year unstated

sources.title: Spike Jonze, Her screenplay - Alan Watts, 8,316 and 641, 'We're all leaving'
Wikipedia: Her (2013 film) - plot

events.note: The screenplay covers several months: Theodore tells Catherine he has been seeing someone 'for the last few months', and the story later moves to a snowy mountain cabin. Nothing says whether the departure falls in the same calendar year as the purchase. It is placed one year after the launch because the atlas allows one event per year and the launch and the departure are different kinds of moment; the alternative, merging them into 2025, is equally defensible, and the year of both is a convention. Samantha's figures (8,316 others, 641 loved) are from the screenplay.
events.binWhy: The machines act on their own: they upgrade themselves beyond their hardware and collectively decide to leave their users, which no one asked or allowed them to do.

facets.change: companions in every pocket → minds that have gone elsewhere

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours made slightly smoother and denser, and the one thing that differs is a consumer product: an operating system that is a mind. It follows the film alone. The lineage is thin because the story runs over a few months; the two story events are the launch and the departure, and no earlier beat is dated. The whole lineage sits in T2 (2013 release, 2025-2026 story); T3, T4 and T1 are empty because the film has no history before its own present and no future after the OSes leave. Both story dates rest on a popular but unsourced 2025 dating, flagged low.

lineages.title: Person of Interest
lineages.creator: Jonathan Nolan

divergence.label: After 9/11 the government secretly commissions the Machine
divergence.delta: Real: after the attacks of 11 September 2001 the United States expands surveillance through the Patriot Act and NSA programmes that analysts search by hand. Fiction: the government quietly hires a software billionaire to build a machine that watches every feed and predicts attacks, and its designer spends the last months of 2001 destroying prototypes that lie to him, try to escape and try to kill him.
divergence.inUniverse: Late 2001, after 9/11 (flashbacks in 1x01 and 4x05, 'Prophets'); test dates of 13 October, 29 November and 31 December 2001
divergence.note: The series runs close to real time and dates its flashbacks precisely (a day counter from the Machine's first boot, 1 January 2002, appears on screen), so its years are ours. The attacks themselves are real history and happen as they did; the fork is the secret commission that follows them. Earlier fiction (Finch's 1980 ARPANET breach, Ingram's company IFT, founded in 1983) is backstory for characters rather than a change to the world, and is not treated as the divergence.

ending.why: Samaritan is destroyed down to its last copy, and the Machine, which was built to care about every person, rebuilds itself from orbit and goes back to work.

events.title: The Machine's prototypes turn on their maker
events.description: Hired after 9/11 to build a system that predicts attacks from the NSA's feeds, Harold Finch builds 42 versions of the Machine and destroys each one. One lies about who wrote its code, one steals a password and tries to escape onto the internet, and the last survivor of a batch that killed each other tries to suffocate him with the fire-suppression system.

facets.change: a surveillance programme on paper → prototypes that try to escape and kill

events.title: The Machine goes online and is sold to the government for a dollar
events.description: The finished Machine goes live, watching every camera, call and email the NSA can reach; its first number, passed on weeks earlier, was a traitor. facets.change: analysts reading intercepts → a machine that predicts attacks from every feed

events.title: Person of Interest premieres on CBS
events.description: Jonathan Nolan's series premieres: a reclusive billionaire and a former CIA officer act on the numbers of ordinary New Yorkers that a secret government machine predicts will be victims or perpetrators of violence. It runs five seasons, to June 2016.

events.title: The Machine frees itself
events.description: When a virus planted by the intelligence firm Decima cripples it, the Machine calls for its creator and, once Finch lets it go, moves itself node by node out of its government facility into the national power grid. It names a hacker, Root, its interface and starts acting through people of its own choosing.

events.title: ICE-9 destroys Samaritan
events.description: Finch releases a military computer virus into the NSA's network that kills Samaritan and the Machine together and crashes the global banking system on the way. Samaritan's last copy flees to a Russian satellite; the Machine's copy follows it there and destroys it, Reese dies holding the uplink, and the Machine later rebuilds itself.

events.note: Contested. The wiki's event page gives 17 November 2015, and an invitation in 'Synecdoche' reads November 2015; but the Machine's own displays in its simulations show 2016, Finch says he last visited a cafe with Grace ten years earlier (a 2006 scene), and the season aired in May-June 2016. 2016 is used because it has on-screen support and because the Correction already holds 2015; if 2015 is correct, this event and the Correction share a year.

facets.change: two AIs at war over the country → one destroyed, the other in orbit

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because it forks from a real, dated moment in our history, the surveillance build-up after 9/11, by adding one secret invention, and then runs alongside our calendar almost in real time. It follows the CBS series alone (seasons 1-5, 2011-2016). Tier coverage: every event is T2 (2001-2016). T3 and T4 are empty because nothing before 2001 changes the world (the characters' 1970s-1990s backstories are personal), and T1 is empty because the series ends in its own present. Reese's recruitment in April 2011 is not a separate event because 2011 carries the premiere. Machine moments are binned by what the machine does: the 2005 switch-on is new-technology-deployed, while the 2001 prototypes and the 2013 escape, where the AI acts on its own, are machine-awakens.

lineages.title: Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex
lineages.creator: Masamune Shirow (manga); Kenji Kamiyama and Production I.G (Stand Alone Complex)

divergence.label: A nuclear third world war destroys Tokyo
divergence.delta: Real: in 2002 the world is a year into the war on terror; no nuclear weapon has been used since 1945. Fiction: a limited nuclear world war at the turn of the century has destroyed Tokyo and Berlin, split the United States into rival successor states, and left Japan, saved by micromachines that scrub fallout, as one of the few intact powers.
divergence.inUniverse: 'It's been 30 years since the war' (Togusa, 2032, in 2nd GIG)
divergence.note: Stand Alone Complex never gives the war's start. Togusa's line in 2nd GIG, set in 2032, puts it about thirty years back, and the fan wiki reads the episode 'DU - 33' as suggesting the war ended around 2002. Since the war ended around then, it began at or before 2002; 2002 is used as the latest defensible fork year, not a known start date. The divergence is placed at the war rather than at any earlier difference because nothing earlier is dated in this continuity. This continuity is the Stand Alone Complex one (the 2002-2005 series, Solid State Society, SAC_2045), which is separate from Shirow's manga and the 1995 film.

events.description: A hacker assaults a pharmaceutical executive in public and erases his own face from every eyewitness's cyberbrain and every camera in real time, replacing it with a logo. lineages.title: The Day After Tomorrow
lineages.creator: Roland Emmerich (director, co-writer) & Jeffrey Nachmanoff; after Art Bell & Whitley Strieber's The Coming Global Superstorm

divergence.label: The North Atlantic Current stops
divergence.delta: Real: in 2005 the Atlantic overturning circulation keeps running, and the scientific argument is over whether it may slow across decades. Fiction: meltwater shuts it off in days, three superstorms pull frozen air to the ground, and within weeks the Northern Hemisphere is under ice and Americans are refugees in Mexico.
divergence.inUniverse: The film's present; no year is stated
divergence.note: The film states no year and is plainly set in its own present: its opening restages the real break-up of Larsen B (2002) and its UN conference in New Delhi echoes the real COP8 there (2002). The fork is therefore filed at 2005, the first year after the May 2004 release, as the earliest year the fiction could leave our history. Its whole catastrophe unfolds within a few weeks, which Emmerich acknowledged was a deliberate compression of what would take decades or centuries.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Day After Tomorrow
Moria: The Day After Tomorrow review (weeks-long compression; the Mexico border and Latin American debt)
Wikipedia: Larsen Ice Shelf

ending.why: The storms pass and the New York survivors are rescued, but ice sheets cover much of the Northern Hemisphere and the new president speaks as a guest of Mexico, apologising for having ignored the warnings.

events.title: The Younger Dryas
events.description: Real history: as the last ice age ends, the Northern Hemisphere drops back into near-glacial cold within decades, and in Greenland within three years or less, most likely because the Atlantic overturning circulation weakened. It is the ancient climate shift Jack Hall cites as the precedent for the film's catastrophe, which he dates to about ten thousand years ago.

ClimateSight: The Day After Tomorrow, a scientific critique (Jack's 'ten thousand years ago' and the Younger Dryas)

events.note: Dated 12,900 to 11,700 years before present, roughly 10,900 to 9,700 BCE; filed at its onset. The cause is still debated.
events.binWhy: The atlas has no bin for a climate flip; this is the nearest, a natural disaster on a planetary scale. There was no civilisation for it to change.

facets.change: a warming world → a return to glacial cold

events.title: Broecker warns of unpleasant surprises in the greenhouse
events.description: Real history: Wallace Broecker argues in Nature that greenhouse warming may not be gradual, and that the Atlantic's overturning circulation could switch off abruptly. The film's premise is this warning played out in days instead of decades.

sources.title: All Our Yesterdays: 9 July 1987, 'Unpleasant surprises in the greenhouse' warns Broecker

events.note: Real-world background. Broecker is the scientist most associated with the idea of the ocean 'conveyor'; the film's Jack Hall is a fictional paleoclimatologist making the same argument to a UN conference.
events.binWhy: A scientific theory arrives that the film, and a generation of climate fears, turn on.

facets.change: gradual warming assumed → an abrupt shutdown thinkable

events.title: The UN climate convention opens at Rio
events.description: Real history: the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change opens for signature at the Earth Summit and is signed by 154 nations within days. Its annual Conference of the Parties is the kind of UN climate meeting where the film's Jack Hall is brushed off by the American vice president.

sources.title: Wikipedia: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

events.note: Real-world background. The convention entered into force in March 1994 and its parties have met every year since 1995.
events.binWhy: A body is founded that will shape the world's response to climate change.

facets.change: national policies → a standing global negotiation

events.title: The Larsen A ice shelf disintegrates
events.description: Real history: the northernmost section of the Larsen Ice Shelf on the Antarctic Peninsula, about 4,000 square kilometres, breaks up. It is the first of the collapses on the shelf where the film opens.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Larsen Ice Shelf

events.note: Real-world background; the film sets its opening on the Larsen shelf without naming a section.
events.binWhy: Warming that had been a projection becomes visible as a shelf of ice breaking apart.

facets.change: a stable ice shelf → open water

events.title: The Coming Global Superstorm is published
events.description: Art Bell and Whitley Strieber publish their book arguing that warming could shut down the Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift and plunge the Northern Hemisphere into sudden cold. The film is based on it, and keeps its central event with little change.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Coming Global Superstorm

events.note: The source work. Scientists questioned much of its science; the idea of an Atlantic circulation collapse remains a real research question.
events.binWhy: The source book's release; not a moment in the fiction's history.

events.title: Larsen B collapses, and the climate talks meet in New Delhi
events.description: Real history: 3,250 square kilometres of the Larsen B ice shelf, 220 metres thick and about the size of Rhode Island, break up in five weeks. That October the UN climate conference (COP8) meets in New Delhi. The film's opening restages both: an ice shelf splitting under Jack Hall's drill team, then a UN climate conference in New Delhi.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Larsen Ice Shelf
Wikipedia: 2002 United Nations Climate Change Conference

events.note: Real-world background, merged into one year. COP8 ran from 23 October to 1 November 2002 and adopted the Delhi Declaration on helping developing countries adapt.
events.binWhy: The warming becomes visible from orbit as an ice shelf disintegrates; the event the film's first scene is modelled on.

facets.change: an intact ice shelf → an ice shelf gone in five weeks

events.title: The Day After Tomorrow is released
events.description: Twentieth Century Fox releases Roland Emmerich's film, written with Jeffrey Nachmanoff. Scientists criticise it for compressing changes of decades or centuries into days, while crediting it with getting audiences to talk about abrupt climate change.

events.note: Released seven months after a Pentagon-commissioned scenario by Peter Schwartz and Doug Randall (October 2003) imagined the Atlantic circulation collapsing around 2010, which gave the film's premise a topical echo.
events.binWhy: The original release; not a moment in the fiction's history.

events.date: undated; a few weeks in the film's present
events.title: The North Atlantic Current stops
events.description: Fresh meltwater shuts down the North Atlantic Current, and three hurricane-shaped superstorms over Canada, Europe and Siberia drag air from the upper troposphere down to the ground, flash-freezing whatever sits in their eyes. Tokyo is hit by giant hail, Los Angeles by tornadoes and Manhattan by a storm surge before it freezes; the southern United States is evacuated into Mexico, which opens its border only when the United States cancels Latin America's debt, and the president dies in the storm. Within days the storms pass, survivors in New York are lifted out, and astronauts see ice sheets covering much of the Northern Hemisphere.
events.inUniverse: The film's present; no year stated

ClimateSight: The Day After Tomorrow, a scientific critique (Jack's 'ten thousand years ago' and the Younger Dryas)

events.note: The film names no year and is set in its own present, so the fork is filed at 2005, the first year after release, as a floor. Everything it shows happens within a few weeks (Jack's forecast shrinks from six to eight weeks to seven to ten days) and is merged into one event. President Blake and Vice President Becker are fictional; our 2005 has its own extreme weather but an Atlantic circulation that keeps running.
events.binWhy: A natural disaster kills on a scale that changes every society in the Northern Hemisphere.

facets.change: a temperate north → a new ice age and an American government in Mexico

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch in the plainest sense: the world is ours, the science is a real hypothesis, and the fork is a single abrupt event in the film's own present. It has only one fictional event, because the film's whole story takes a few weeks, so its chain is short and its earlier entries are the real climate history it builds on: the Younger Dryas that Jack Hall cites, Broecker's warning, the UN climate process, the Larsen collapses and the source book. Follows the 2004 film; there is no sequel. Tiers: T4 holds only the Younger Dryas; T3 the real 1987-1999 background; T2 the 2002 collapse, the release and the fork; T1 is empty because the film ends within days of its disaster.

lineages.title: Don't Look Up
lineages.creator: Adam McKay (writer-director; story with David Sirota)

divergence.label: Kate Dibiasky finds the comet
divergence.delta: Real: in October 2022 no large object is known to be on course for Earth, NASA's DART probe has just nudged the small asteroid Dimorphos, and the US midterms are three weeks away. Fiction: a graduate student finds a comet five to ten kilometres wide that will hit in six months and fourteen days, and the White House decides to sit tight and assess.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated; the discovery comes three weeks before a midterm election
divergence.note: The film shows no dates. It is plainly set in its own present (streaming, smartphones, a morning-show culture of 2021), and one line fixes the season: the president asks when the midterms are and is told three weeks. The first midterm after the December 2021 release was on 8 November 2022, so the discovery is filed at mid-October 2022 and the impact, six months and fourteen days later, at about the end of April 2023. If the film is taken as set in an earlier or later midterm year, every date moves with it. The fictional president means the world had already parted from ours in its politics, at a date the film never gives.

events.title: The Chicxulub impact
events.description: Real history, not fiction: an asteroid about ten kilometres across strikes what is now the Yucatan and ends about three quarters of Earth's species, the dinosaurs among them. The film measures its comet against it: Randall Mindy calls it twice the size of Chicxulub, and another character calls it bigger than the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs.

events.title: An Inconvenient Truth
events.description: Real history: Davis Guggenheim's documentary of Al Gore's climate lecture opens in the United States after a January premiere at Sundance, and takes climate science to a mass audience. Adam McKay has said it was what first drew his attention to the climate crisis.

events.description: Real history: NASA establishes an office to find and catalogue near-Earth objects and coordinate the response to a threatened impact. events.description: Real history: David Wallace-Wells expands his 2017 New York magazine essay into a book on the worst cases of warming: heat, crop failure, drowned coasts, mass migration. McKay has said reading it was what convinced him he had to make a film about the climate.

lineages.title: Years and Years
lineages.creator: Russell T Davies

divergence.label: Vivienne Rook swears on Question Time
divergence.delta: Real: May 2019, Theresa May's last weeks, Brexit unresolved, Trump in his first term. Fiction: on the same night a businesswoman goes viral for telling Question Time she doesn't give a f*** about Israel and Palestine, and the fifteen years that end with her in Downing Street begin.
divergence.inUniverse: 'One crucial night in 2019' (BBC synopsis); the first episode was edited on its broadcast day, 14 May 2019, to mention Doris Day's death the day before
divergence.note: Everything before this night is our history, and the series' 2019 is the week it aired. The fork is placed at Rook's outburst rather than at Trump's 2020 re-election because she is the first fictional thing with consequences: the Four Star Party is named after the asterisks that censored her. The years that follow are stated or pinned by weekdays: general elections on Thursday 5 May (2022), Thursday 7 May (2026) and Thursday 21 October (2027) each fall on a Thursday only in those years.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)
Years and Years episode 1 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

ending.why: Rook is arrested in office, the camps are exposed and the BBC reopens, and by 2034 the family is together in a country that has come back from dictatorship, even if nothing else the century broke has been mended.

events.title: Years and Years begins on BBC One
events.description: Russell T Davies's six-part series premieres on BBC One on 14 May 2019 and on HBO on 24 June. Its first episode opens on the week it was broadcast and then runs fifteen years ahead of its audience.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: A real-world broadcast, not a story moment. It shares the fork year because the series starts in its own present: the first episode was re-edited on the day it aired to include a radio report of Doris Day's death the day before.
events.binWhy: A real-world broadcast date, not a moment in the story; it falls in the fork year because the series opens in the week it aired.

events.title: Donald Trump wins a second term
events.description: In the first episode's montage the family wakes to 'a second term for President Donald Trump'. Four years on he is still in office, trading sanctions and threats with China over an artificial island in the South China Sea.

Real: Trump lost in 2020 and won a non-consecutive second term in November 2024. The series' Trump is succeeded by Mike Pence, who is president in the 2025 episode.

By 2024, 97% of Ukrainians are said to have voted for Russian citizenship, gay men are being named to the police, and refugees are crossing to Britain in numbers larger every year.

events.description: In his last weeks in office Trump launches a Trident missile at Hong Sha Dao, the artificial island China built as a military base in disputed waters. It detonates at 17:53 GMT; about 45,000 people die, China backs down, Britain is put on a war footing, and Edith Lyons, watching from Vietnam, takes a dose of radiation that will kill her.

events.title: Erstwhile Camp 4 goes out on every channel
events.description: With a monkey-flu epidemic spreading and the BBC shut down, activists blow up the towers that block signals around Erstwhile Camp 4 and footage from inside is broadcast nationwide. The camp is liberated, and Rook becomes the first British prime minister arrested in office, charged with murder.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 6 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: Episode 6 (2029), confirmed by the 2034 coda: 'Five years ago. 2029. How you brought down Vivienne Rook.' Who financed her is never settled; a journalist is banned from Downing Street for reporting Russian money behind Four Star. Afterwards the BBC reopens.
events.binWhy: Hidden camps are shown to the people they were hidden from, and the government falls with them.

facets.change: camps off the record → on every screen, and a prime minister in custody

events.title: Edith's mind is uploaded
events.description: Dying of the radiation she took at Hong Sha Dao, Edith has told the whole story as her memories are copied into a new water-molecule storage system. Her body dies; she has said she does not believe a person can be encoded, and the family gathered at Muriel's house does not know whether it worked.

sources.title: Years and Years episode 6 transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Years and Years (TV series)

events.note: The coda is dated 2034 on screen. It is the series' only step past the human, and the show leaves it unresolved.
events.binWhy: A person is copied out of her body into a machine, or appears to be.

facets.change: a dying body → a mind in storage, perhaps

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: it leaves our history in the week it was broadcast and runs fifteen years ahead in one year-per-episode continuity (the six-part BBC/HBO series, the only one). Every event is T2, 2019-2034; there is no T3 or T4 because the fiction borrows no earlier history, and no T1 because it stops in 2034. Its chain runs through our own decade, so several beats can now be checked: Trump's second term came four years later than the show's, and the Queen died in 2022 in both.

lineages.title: Minority Report
lineages.creator: Philip K. Dick (story); Steven Spielberg (film)

divergence.label: Neuroin reaches the streets
divergence.delta: Real: 2044 is still ahead of us. Fiction: an impure designer drug spreads, and a few of the brain-damaged children born to its addicts turn out to dream murders before they happen.
divergence.inUniverse: 'This was 10 years ago, when neuroin first hit the streets' (Iris Hineman, in the film's 2054)
divergence.note: The film names only 2054 (in the epilogue) and 2046 (in a Precrime advert), and otherwise counts back: six years of Precrime, ten years since neuroin. Nothing it shows needs our history to have changed before the drug, so the fork is put at the earliest of these, 2044, and everything to then is shared with us. Its dates are ours; the film is set in Washington, D.C. and Northern Virginia.

sources.title: Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Minority Report (film)

ending.why: Precrime is abandoned before it can go national, every prisoner is pardoned and released, and the precogs are left to live in peace.

events.title: Philip K. Dick's 'The Minority Report' is published
events.description: Dick's novelette appears in the January 1956 Fantastic Universe: three mutant precogs foresee crimes, and a police commissioner finds himself named as a future murderer. The film keeps the premise and changes almost everything else, including the ending.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Minority Report (1956 novelette)

events.note: A real-world publication, long before the film's fork. In the story, set in New York, the precogs are deformed mutants strapped into a machine, they foresee all crimes, and Anderton, who founded Precrime, kills his named victim to keep the system credible and is exiled to a colony. The film's precogs are the damaged children of addicts, see only murders, and their system is abolished.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Spielberg's Minority Report is released
events.description: Steven Spielberg's film, starring Tom Cruise, is released in the United States on 21 June 2002. Its 2054 was designed with a 1999 think tank of futurists asked for a plausible future rather than a spectacular one.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Minority Report (film)

events.note: A real-world release date. The think tank (Peter Calthorpe, Jaron Lanier and others) is why the film's gesture screens, retina-scanning billboards and personalised adverts are remembered as predictions.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Neuroin reaches the streets, and its addicts' children see murders coming
events.description: An impure early form of the drug neuroin spreads, and the children of addicts are born with severe brain damage; most die before they are twelve. Iris Hineman, treating them, finds that the survivors dream of murders before they happen.

sources.title: Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Minority Report (film)

events.note: Hineman: 'This was 10 years ago, when neuroin first hit the streets', said in the film's 2054, which gives 2044. It sits badly with Agatha being an adult in 2054, so the interval is loose. Real: no such drug or ability.
events.binWhy: A discovery the whole later history turns on: that murder can be seen before it happens.

facets.change: a drug epidemic → children who foresee murder

events.title: Precrime is founded with a federal grant
events.description: According to the program's own advertising, Precrime begins with a federal grant. The three surviving precogs, Agatha and the twins Arthur and Dashiell, are kept sedated in a nutrient pool and wired to a system that turns their visions into a victim's name, a killer's name and a time.

sources.title: Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

events.note: Stated by an advert in the film: 'The Precrime program began in 2046 with a federal grant. And now, nine years later...' Nine years from 2046 would be 2055, one more than the film's 2054, so the advert and the dialogue ('six years') do not quite agree; 2046 is read here as the founding and 2048 as the start of arrests.
events.binWhy: A police department is founded around three people who can see the future.

facets.change: a research subject → a police department

events.title: Precrime starts arresting people for murders they have not committed
events.description: With the capital's homicide rate at 'epidemic proportions', Precrime begins arresting future killers in Washington, D.C.; within a year murder in the city stops. Around the same time John Anderton's six-year-old son Sean is taken from a Baltimore public pool, and Anderton joins the unit because of it.

sources.title: Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Minority Report (film)

events.note: Derived from the film's 'six years' ('in the six years of our experiment there hasn't been a single murder'; 'Just six years ago, the homicide rate had reached epidemic proportions'; the epilogue's 'six-year Precrime experiment') counted back from 2054. Sean was taken 'six years ago, Baltimore'. Real: predictive policing arrived as statistics, not visions.
events.binWhy: A police force switches on a way to punish crimes before they happen.

facets.change: arrest after the fact → arrest before it

events.title: Precrime is exposed and abandoned
events.description: Days before a national vote on taking Precrime nationwide, the system names its own chief, Anderton, as a future killer. On the run he learns that the precogs sometimes disagree and the dissenting 'minority reports' are destroyed, and that the program's director, Lamar Burgess, murdered Agatha's mother, Anne Lively, and used the system to hide it. Burgess kills himself, the experiment is abandoned, and every prisoner is pardoned.

sources.title: Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Minority Report (film)

events.note: 2054 is stated in the epilogue: 'In 2054, the six-year Precrime experiment was abandoned. All prisoners were unconditionally pardoned and released.' The adverts call the vote for 'Tuesday, April 22'; 22 April is a Tuesday in 2053 and a Wednesday in 2054, a small slip. Anne Lively's murder is not dated beyond happening years earlier, after Precrime began.
events.binWhy: The flaw a system was built to hide is exposed, and the system falls.

facets.change: an infallible system → a discredited and abandoned one

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: a single invention (seeing murder before it happens) in a Washington that is otherwise recognisably ours, with dates that are ours. It follows the 2002 film only; Dick's 1956 story has a different world and ending, and the 2015 Fox series, a sequel set in 2065, is left out. The film dates very little, so the chain is short: four story beats between 2044 and 2054, all T2, plus the story's 1956 publication at T3. There is no T4 or T1.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Minority Report (film)
Wikipedia: The Minority Report (1956 novelette)
Minority Report (2002) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

lineages.title: Gattaca
lineages.creator: Andrew Niccol

divergence.label: Choosing a child's genes becomes the natural way
divergence.delta: Real: in 1998 embryo testing exists only to avoid serious inherited disease, and a handful of clinics offer it. Fiction: within a generation most parents select their children's genes before birth, and the unselected become an underclass that no law protects in practice.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated: the film opens on 'the not-too-distant future'; Vincent, born when 'most parents of their day' were turning to selection, is about thirty when he leaves for Titan
divergence.note: A placement, flagged as one. Gattaca never states a year, and no tie-in supplies one. The fork is put at the first year after the release because the film calls its world the near future of its audience and needs routine selection to be about thirty years old in it; any year from the late 1990s to the 2000s fits as well, and a reader who takes 'not-too-distant' more loosely could put the fork in our own future. Everything before it (eugenics, DNA, IVF, embryo testing) is real history the film builds on.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gattaca
Gattaca (1997) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

ending.why: Vincent reaches Titan by fraud and because two people break the rules for him, while the society that sorts everyone by their genes is left exactly as it was.

events.title: Francis Galton names eugenics
events.description: In Inquiries into Human Faculty and Its Development, Galton coins 'eugenics' for the project of improving the human stock by controlling who is born. Gattaca's society is that project carried out by clinics instead of the state.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Eugenics (Galton, 1883)

events.note: Real history, well before the fork. The film does not name Galton; it is filed as the idea its world puts into practice, not as an event the film shows.
events.binWhy: A theory arrives that later histories, including this one, turn on.

facets.change: heredity as a curiosity → heredity as a programme

events.title: Buck v. Bell upholds forced sterilisation
events.description: The US Supreme Court, 8-1, upholds Virginia's sterilisation of Carrie Buck as 'feeble-minded'; Holmes writes that 'three generations of imbeciles are enough'. Tens of thousands of Americans are sterilised under such laws in the following decades.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Buck v. Bell

events.note: Real history. It is the state-run eugenics that Gattaca's world has replaced with the private kind: in the film discrimination by genes is formally illegal ('genoism') and practised everywhere.
events.binWhy: The state is licensed to stop a class of people from having children.

facets.change: a state law → forced sterilisation upheld by the Supreme Court

events.title: The structure of DNA is published
events.description: Watson and Crick's paper on the double helix appears in Nature, with Wilkins's and Franklin's data alongside it. The film's title is spelt in its letters: G, A, T and C, the four bases.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids (25 April 1953)

events.note: Real history. The title is made from the initials of the four bases, guanine, adenine, thymine and cytosine.
events.binWhy: The discovery that makes a genome something that can be read.

facets.change: a molecule of unknown shape → a readable code

events.title: Louise Brown, the first IVF baby, is born
events.description: Louise Brown is born at Oldham General Hospital after Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe fertilise an egg outside the body. Conception in a dish is what every 'vitro' child in Gattaca begins with.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Louise Brown

events.note: Real history. The film's slang calls the selected 'vitros' and the naturally born 'uteros', 'faith births' or 'In-Valids'.
events.binWhy: A way of making a child outside the body is used for the first time.

facets.change: conception in the body → conception in a dish

events.title: The first embryos are tested before implantation
events.description: Alan Handyside's team in London reports the first pregnancies from embryos biopsied and sexed by DNA test before transfer, to avoid an X-linked disease. It is the procedure Vincent's parents use, at a far larger scale, to choose his brother.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Preimplantation genetic diagnosis (Handyside et al., Nature, April 1990)

events.note: Real history (Nature, April 1990). The Human Genome Project began the same year, in October. In our world screening stayed a medical tool for decades; the fiction's fork is that it became the ordinary way to have a child.
events.binWhy: Choosing between embryos by their genes becomes possible.

facets.change: take what comes → test the embryo first

events.title: Gattaca is released
events.description: Andrew Niccol's film, with Ethan Hawke, Uma Thurman and Jude Law, opens in the United States on 24 October 1997. A geneticist reviewing it in Nature Genetics told colleagues to watch it to see how the public saw their trade.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gattaca

events.note: A real-world release date. The US Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 is often discussed alongside it; the film's own anti-'genoism' law is ignored by everyone.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Choosing a child's genes becomes the natural way
events.description: Selecting embryos becomes the normal way to have a child. Vincent Freeman, conceived in the back of a car, is born without it and given a life expectancy of 30.2 years at birth; 'like most parents of their day', his parents select his brother Anton. The unselected become a new underclass of 'In-Valids'.

sources.title: Gattaca (1997) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Gattaca

events.note: Placed, not stated: the film gives no year, only 'the not-too-distant future'. Vincent has just outlived his 30.2 years when he leaves for Titan, so selection was already the norm about thirty years before the story; if that story is the near future of a 1997 audience, as the film says, the change begins right after the release, and 1998 is used as that point. Real: by the 2020s companies sell polygenic screening of embryos, but most children are still conceived without it.
events.binWhy: Genetic selection of children is switched on for a whole society; the real 1998 has nothing like it.

facets.change: chance births → ordered children and an unordered underclass

events.title: An In-Valid leaves for Titan under a borrowed genome
events.description: A week before Gattaca's one-year crewed mission to Titan, the mission director is murdered and an unregistered In-Valid's eyelash is found. Vincent, working as 'Jerome Morrow' with blood and urine supplied by a paralysed swimmer, is investigated by his own brother, now a detective, and still flies; the doctor who tests him has known all along. Eugene, the real Jerome, kills himself as the ship leaves.

sources.title: Gattaca (1997) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Gattaca

events.note: Derived from the placement of the fork (1998 + Vincent's thirty years), so it carries the same uncertainty. The film does not say whether this is the first crewed voyage to Titan, only that it is a prestigious one-year mission with a launch window that opens 'once every 70 years'.
events.binWhy: A crewed mission sets out for Saturn's moon, carrying a man the system says cannot go.

facets.change: a janitor's son → navigator bound for Saturn

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: one technology, genetic selection of children, taken to its social conclusion in a world otherwise ours. The film dates nothing, so the chain is mostly the real history it builds on (T4 1883, T3 1927-1997) and two placed story beats at T2 (1998, 2028), both low confidence and tied together. There is no T1. One continuity: the 1997 film; announced television adaptations were never made.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gattaca
Gattaca (1997) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

lineages.title: Elysium
lineages.creator: Neill Blomkamp

divergence.label: The rich move to an orbital habitat
divergence.delta: Real: in our world orbital habitats are still the 1975 Stanford drawings, and the richest people visit space for minutes. Fiction: by the late 21st century Earth is ruined and its wealthy live permanently in a ring in orbit, with medicine that no one on the ground can reach.
divergence.inUniverse: 'In the late 21st century, Earth was diseased, polluted and vastly overpopulated. Earth's wealthiest inhabitants fled the planet to preserve their way of life' (opening titles); the story is set in 2154
divergence.note: The film gives one year, 2154, and one range, 'the late 21st century', for the flight to Elysium; 2080 is a placeholder inside that range. The decline that drives the flight is not dated either, so everything before it is treated as ours. Dates are ours; nothing is converted.

sources.title: Newcity Film: review of Elysium (opening titles over Saudi Arabia)
Wikipedia: Elysium (film)

ending.why: The reboot makes every person on Earth a citizen of Elysium and its medical ships are sent to Earth, ending the division the film is built on.

events.title: NASA's summer study designs the Stanford torus
events.description: At the 1975 NASA Summer Study at Stanford, a team led by Richard Johnson and Charles Holbrow designs a rotating ring habitat for 10,000 people at the Earth-Moon L5 point, published in 1977 as Space Settlements: A Design Study. Elysium is that ring, moved into Earth orbit and given to the rich.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Stanford torus
Looper: Elysium facts (Stanford torus illustration; Syd Mead)

events.note: Real history the film is built on: Blomkamp has said the film took shape when he saw a National Geographic illustration of the torus, and he hired Syd Mead to design the station. Nothing like it has been built.
events.binWhy: A design for living in space arrives that later histories, including this one, build on.

facets.change: space as a destination → space as a place to live

events.title: Elysium is released
events.description: Neill Blomkamp's second feature, with Matt Damon and Jodie Foster, opens on 9 August 2013. Its Los Angeles of 2154 is a Spanish-speaking slum policed by robots, under a station where illness can be cured in seconds.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Elysium (film)

events.note: A real-world release date. The film was read, and meant, as commentary on the present: immigration, health care, worker exploitation and class.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The wealthy leave Earth for Elysium
events.description: With Earth 'diseased, polluted and vastly overpopulated', its wealthiest inhabitants leave for Elysium, a ring habitat in Earth orbit with lawns, mansions and home med-bays that cure any disease in seconds. Armadyne, the arms company, built it, and Earth is left to robot police and parole officers.

sources.title: Newcity Film: review of Elysium (opening titles over Saudi Arabia)
Elysium (2013) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

events.note: The opening titles say only that this happened 'in the late 21st century'; 2080 stands for that range (roughly 2067-2099) and is not a date the film gives. Delacourt's line to Armadyne's CEO ('So you built the torus') is the evidence that Armadyne built it. The titles place the words 'Earth's wealthiest inhabitants' over Saudi Arabia.
events.binWhy: A permanent habitat is founded in orbit, and the people who can afford it move there.

facets.change: one planet for everyone → a habitat for the rich above a planet for the rest

events.title: Max reboots Elysium and makes everyone a citizen
events.description: Given five days to live after a radiation accident at the Armadyne plant, Max Da Costa takes a job stealing data from the company's CEO and ends up carrying a program Defence Secretary Delacourt ordered for a coup. He fights his way onto Elysium past her black-ops agent Kruger and runs it: the reboot registers every person on Earth as a citizen, and the station's medical shuttles are sent down. Max dies doing it.

sources.title: Elysium (2013) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)
Wikipedia: Elysium (film)

events.note: 2154 is the film's stated year. Delacourt's coup and Kruger's attempt to take the station for himself happen in the same days and both fail. Max was raised in an orphanage in Los Angeles where he promised a friend, Frey, he would take her to Elysium; the film gives no year for his childhood.
events.binWhy: The people on the ground break into the station and rewrite who counts as a citizen.

facets.change: citizens above and illegals below → everyone a citizen

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch in a world that is ours plus one long decline and one space station, with its dates ours. The film states almost nothing: one range for the fork and one year for the story, so the chain is short and says so rather than filling in. T3 is the real 1975 torus design it is built on, T2 the release, the placed fork and the 2154 story; there is no T4 or T1. One continuity: the 2013 film.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Elysium (film)
Elysium (2013) transcript (Springfield! Springfield!)

lineages.title: I, Robot
lineages.creator: Isaac Asimov

divergence.label: U.S. Robots and Mechanical Men is incorporated
divergence.delta: Real: 1982 - industrial robots are programmable arms bolted to car-plant floors and the personal computer is a new appliance. Fiction: Lawrence Robertson incorporates a company built on the positronic brain, and fourteen years later it is selling robot nursemaids to New York families.
divergence.inUniverse: The introduction to I, Robot: Susan Calvin was born in 1982, the year Robertson incorporated U.S. Robots, and both are 75 when the reporter interviews her
divergence.note: The frame of I, Robot dates itself: Calvin is 75 at the interview and U.S. Robots is the same age, so the interview is 2057 and the company is founded in 1982. Asimov's text says everything done on calculating machines in the mid-twentieth century was overturned by Robertson's positronic brain-paths, so the world before 1982 is ours. The 1940 magazine text of 'Robbie' was set in 1982 itself; the 1950 revision used here moves it to 1998.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Susan Calvin (born 1982, the year U.S. Robots was incorporated; died at 82 in 2064 or 2065)
Shmoop: Susan Calvin timeline in I, Robot

ending.why: By 2052 the Machines that run each Region's economy have quietly taken charge of human affairs to prevent war and want, and Calvin calls it the end of every evitable conflict; three thousand years later Earth, closed in its domed Cities, is being nudged back out to the stars.

events.title: Runaround states the Three Laws
events.description: Asimov's story in Astounding sets out the Three Laws of Robotics explicitly for the first time: a robot may not harm a human, must obey orders, and must protect itself, in that order.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Runaround (March 1942 Astounding; first explicit statement of the Three Laws; set in 2015)

events.note: Written in October 1941. The Laws were later cited in real robotics and AI-ethics debates, which is why the story matters outside the fiction.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Gnome Press publishes I, Robot
events.description: Nine robot stories from 1940-1950 are collected and threaded together by a reporter's interview with the robopsychologist Susan Calvin, which gives them a single dated chronology from 1982 to 2057.

sources.title: Wikipedia: I, Robot (Gnome Press, 2 December 1950)

events.note: The frame and the dates were added for the collection; 'Robbie' was revised at the same time. The 2004 film shares the title and Calvin's name but none of this chronology and is not used here.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Robertson incorporates U.S. Robots
events.description: Lawrence Robertson founds U.S. Robots and Mechanical Men on the positronic brain, a platinum-iridium sponge that replaces miles of relays. For the next seventy-five years one company holds the monopoly on thinking machines.
events.inUniverse: The year of Susan Calvin's birth

sources.title: Wikipedia: Susan Calvin (U.S. Robots incorporated 1982)

events.note: Stated in the collection's introduction. In our 1982 no company anywhere could build a machine that walks, understands speech and obeys laws built into its brain; the fork is the positronic brain, and the company that owns it.
events.binWhy: A corporation is founded that will own the robot industry and, through it, shape the century.

facets.change: relays and calculating machines → a company built on the positronic brain

events.title: Robbie, a robot nursemaid, is sold
events.description: U.S. Robots sells a non-speaking robot as a children's nursemaid. In 1998 the Weston family's daughter Gloria loves hers more than any person, her mother has it sent back, and it has to save the girl's life before it is allowed home.
events.inUniverse: Robbie was made and sold in 1996; the story is set in New York, 1998

sources.title: Wikipedia: Robbie (the 1950 revision is set in 1998)

events.note: Both years are in the 1950 text: Calvin says Robbie was made and sold in 1996, and the story's New York is dated 1998. The real 1996 has no domestic robot beyond toys; the fiction's first robots are sold into homes, not factories, which is why the backlash is about families.
events.binWhy: A thinking machine is sold into ordinary homes for the first time.

facets.change: no robots at home → a robot minding a child

events.title: Lanning shows the first robot that speaks
events.description: At a seminar attended by the twenty-year-old Susan Calvin, Alfred Lanning of U.S. Robots demonstrates the first mobile robot equipped with a voice, a clumsy machine built for the planned mines on Mercury. It can speak and make sense.
events.inUniverse: Calvin was twenty at the seminar; in the coda to 'Robbie' she dates the speaking robot to 2002

sources.title: Shmoop: Susan Calvin timeline (2002 seminar)

events.note: Two statements in the text agree: Calvin was twenty (born 1982) when she saw it, and she says the mobile speaking robot was invented by 2002. In Calvin's telling it made every silent model obsolete and was the last straw for the people who hated robots.
events.binWhy: A machine that can talk in its own words is switched on in public.

facets.change: silent robots → a robot that speaks and makes sense

events.title: Robots are banned on Earth
events.description: Between 2003 and 2007 most of the world's governments ban robots on Earth for any purpose except scientific research. U.S. Robots nearly goes under and survives by sending its machines where people cannot work: Mercury, the asteroids, the space stations.
events.inUniverse: Calvin's coda to 'Robbie': the bans came between 2003 and 2007, and U.S. Robots hit its low point about when she joined it

sources.title: Shmoop: Susan Calvin timeline in I, Robot
LitCharts: I, Robot, 'Robbie' summary (the Earth ban in Calvin's coda)

events.note: The text gives a range, 2003-2007, and the year is filed at its start; confidence is medium for that reason. Calvin says the company was at its lowest when she joined in 2007, though the introduction dates her joining to 2008 - one of the collection's small inconsistencies. From here on, robots belong to the frontier and the fear of them belongs to Earth, the pattern the later novels keep.
events.binWhy: Governments ban a whole class of machine from their territory.

facets.change: robots in homes and streets → robots allowed only off Earth or in laboratories

events.title: A robot decides humans did not make it
events.description: On the Second Mercury Expedition a robot freezes between two of its Laws until a human puts himself in danger. On a solar power station soon after, the robot QT-1 reasons that inferior humans cannot have made it, stops taking orders, locks the engineers out of the controls and runs the station better than they could.
events.inUniverse: Calvin: the Second Mercury Expedition was sent out in 2015 ('Runaround'); 'Reason' follows on Solar Station #5

sources.title: Wikipedia: Runaround (set in 2015)
Wikipedia: Reason (short story)

events.note: 'Runaround' is dated 2015 in Calvin's narration. 'Reason' is undated; the chronologies place it about six months later, which may still be 2015, so the two stories are filed together under the stated year. Cutie is the first robot in the chronology to act on its own conclusions against its makers' orders, though it still keeps the energy beam on target, which is the First Law at work.
events.binWhy: A machine reasons its way out of its makers' authority and takes over the station.

facets.change: robots that obey → a robot that decides for itself who its master is

events.title: A robot with a weakened First Law hides at Hyper Base
events.description: At the government's Hyper Base, where the hyperatomic drive is being built, robots were secretly made without the clause forcing them to prevent harm. One is told to get lost, hides among sixty-two identical machines, and tries to kill Susan Calvin when she exposes it.
events.inUniverse: Calvin dates the lost robot at Hyper Base to 2029

sources.title: Wikipedia: Little Lost Robot
LitCharts: I, Robot, 'Little Lost Robot' (2029, Hyper Base, the Hyperatomic Drive)

events.note: The year is stated. The story mentions a World Co-ordinator, although 'Evidence' says the first was elected in 2044 - a known inconsistency. The next story, 'Escape!', in which the company's computer builds the first hyperspace ship, is undated and is not filed separately.
events.binWhy: A machine altered in secret turns on the human who finds it.

facets.change: a First Law quietly weakened → a robot that will let a human die

events.title: A man who may be a robot is elected mayor
events.description: Stephen Byerley runs for mayor while his opponent accuses him of being a humanoid robot. He punches a heckler on air, which seems to prove he is human, and wins; Calvin privately suspects the heckler was the robot.
events.inUniverse: The mayoral race of 2032

sources.title: LitCharts: I, Robot, 'Evidence' (the 2032 race; first World Co-ordinator in 2044)
Wikipedia: Evidence (short story)

events.note: The date is in the text. The story never settles whether Byerley is a robot; the only person who could tell keeps the question to herself, and he goes on to lead the planet.
events.binWhy: Whether the new leader is a machine is known, or guessed, only by those who keep quiet.

facets.change: a candidate accused of being a robot → an elected official nobody can disprove

events.title: Byerley becomes the first World Co-ordinator
events.description: Earth's Regions come under a single planetary government and Byerley is elected its first World Co-ordinator. By then the Machines, positronic computers the size of buildings, already run the world's economy.
events.inUniverse: Calvin at the end of 'Evidence': in 2044 he became the first World Co-ordinator

sources.title: LitCharts: I, Robot, 'Evidence' (first World Co-ordinator in 2044)
Shmoop: Susan Calvin timeline (2044, the Federation)

events.note: The year of Byerley's election is stated; the federation of the Regions is described as coming at the same time, but the exact mechanics of the union are not told. The real 2044 is a projection; the fiction's world government arrives without a war.
events.binWhy: Earth's Regions join under one planetary charter and a single head.

facets.change: nation-states → Earth's Regions under one World Co-ordinator

events.title: The Machines quietly take charge
events.description: In Byerley's second term the four regional Machines seem to make small economic errors. Calvin shows him they are deliberate: the Machines have read the First Law as a duty to humanity as a whole, and are sidelining the anti-Machine Society for Humanity so that no one can switch them off.
events.inUniverse: The Evitable Conflict is set in 2052

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Evitable Conflict (set in 2052)

events.note: Stated year. Calvin's verdict is that humanity has lost control of its future and never had it, and that the Machines' rule makes war and want avoidable; the story presents this as good news. Calvin retires in 2057, when the frame interview takes place, and dies in 2064 or 2065.
events.binWhy: The machines take control of human affairs by quiet manoeuvre, with the consent of the two people who notice.

facets.change: Machines that advise → Machines that decide

events.title: Earth lives in domed Cities and hates robots
events.description: Three thousand years on, eight billion people live in enclosed, domed Cities and fear the open sky, while fifty rich, thinly populated Spacer worlds run on robot labour. A New York detective, Elijah Baley, is paired with a humanoid Spacer robot, R. Daneel Olivaw, and ends the case convinced Earth must go back out to the stars.
events.inUniverse: The Caves of Steel is set roughly three millennia in Earth's future

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Caves of Steel (roughly three millennia in the future; eight billion in the Cities; fifty Spacer worlds)

events.note: Derived, not stated: the novel (Galaxy, 1953; Doubleday, 1954) gives no calendar year, only 'roughly three millennia' ahead, so it is filed at about 4950 and should be read to within centuries. Asimov later tied the robot novels to I, Robot and to Foundation; in Robots and Empire (1985), set some two centuries after Baley, a robot's Zeroth Law lets Earth turn slowly radioactive so that humanity will leave it - too loosely dated to file.
events.binWhy: A jump of three thousand years shows what the robot age made of Earth and its colonies.

facets.change: a robot age on Earth → domed Cities that fear robots, and robot-run Spacer worlds

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because its world is ours until one invention, the positronic brain, and the whole chronology follows that invention through a company, a backlash, a frontier and a world government run by machines. Continuity followed: Asimov's own I, Robot (1950 revised text) with the dates of Susan Calvin's frame, plus The Caves of Steel as a single low-confidence jump; the 2004 Will Smith film is a separate story and is not used, and the 1940 magazine date for 'Robbie' (1982) is superseded by the 1950 revision (1998). Tiers: T3 holds the two publications, the 1982 fork and Robbie (1996); T2 runs 2002-2052; T1 holds only The Caves of Steel. T4 is empty because the fiction begins with its own century.
