lineages.title: Altered Carbon
lineages.creator: Richard K. Morgan

divergence.label: The first Martian datasystems are decoded
divergence.delta: Real: Mars has been searched for ruins since the Viking photographs of 1976, and has shown only rock. Fiction: by 2089 a dig at Bradbury on Mars has found the remains of a starfaring culture as old as humanity, and its archives include charts of the habitable worlds it once settled.
divergence.inUniverse: 'Bradbury, 2089 precolonial reckoning' - the heading of a passage in Broken Angels on the decoding of the first Martian datasystems
divergence.note: The novels give almost no Earth-calendar dates. 2089 is the one stated year that marks a change of history: Broken Angels (pp. 332-33) dates the decoding of the first Martian datasystems to '2089 precolonial reckoning', after which humans know which stars to send ships to. Altered Carbon also mentions the Hendrix hotel opening in 2087, and the dig at Bradbury is older than 2089 but undated; neither is a departure of substance, so the fork is placed at the decoding.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Takeshi Kovacs (cites Broken Angels pp. 332-36: '2089 pre-colonial reckoning', 'over four centuries of archaeology'; the novels are set in or around the 26th century)
Bram reads books: Broken Angels review (quotes the 'Bradbury, 2089 precolonial reckoning' passage)

ending.why: Woken Furies ends with Quellcrist Falconer's recorded mind alive in another woman's body, a link to the Martian orbital guns and a dormant gene weapon aimed at the ruling families, and stops before the revolution is fought.

events.title: Viking 1 lands on Mars and photographs a 'face'
events.description: Viking 1 becomes the first spacecraft to land and work on Mars, on 20 July 1976. Five days later its orbiter photographs a two-kilometre mesa in Cydonia that looks like a human face, and the idea of ruins on Mars gets its most famous picture.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Viking 1 (landed 20 July 1976, the first successful Mars lander)
Wikipedia: Cydonia (Mars) (the 'face' photographed 25 July 1976)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork as the ground the novels' Martian premise stands on; Morgan does not cite Viking. The dig in the novels is named Bradbury, after Ray Bradbury's dead Martian civilisation.
events.binWhy: The first working landing on Mars, and the first photograph that made people look for ruins there.

facets.change: Mars seen from a distance → Mars from its surface, and a 'face' at Cydonia

events.title: Dolly, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell
events.description: A sheep cloned from an adult somatic cell is born at the Roslin Institute in Scotland and announced the following February. It shows a mature cell can be reprogrammed to grow a whole new body.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dolly (sheep) (born 5 July 1996, announced 22 February 1997)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The novels' rich keep banks of cloned bodies, 'sleeves', grown from their own cells; the real limit is that a clone is a new body with no mind in it, which is the gap the fiction's cortical stack fills.
events.binWhy: Cloning a body from an adult cell is shown to work.

facets.change: clones from embryos only → a mammal grown from an adult cell

events.title: The 'face on Mars' is shown to be a hill
events.description: Mars Global Surveyor photographs the Cydonia mesa at high resolution, and it turns out to be an ordinary eroded hill whose face appears only at one angle of light.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cydonia (Mars) (April 2001 MOC image; a natural hill)

events.note: Real history, a year before the novel. It is the real world's answer to the question the fiction answers the other way: we looked for Martian ruins and found a hill; the books' archaeologists find a civilisation.
events.binWhy: A higher-resolution image exposes the 'face' as a trick of the light.

facets.change: a face on Mars → a hill on Mars

events.title: Gollancz publishes Altered Carbon
events.description: Richard K. Morgan's first novel puts an interstellar soldier into a borrowed body in Bay City, formerly San Francisco, to solve the death of a man who cannot stay dead. Broken Angels (2003) and Woken Furies (2005) follow.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Altered Carbon (published 28 February 2002)

events.note: The novel won the 2003 Philip K. Dick Award. Netflix adapted it in 2018 with its own dates (2384, and 2414 for season 2) and a different backstory for Kovacs and Falconer; that continuity is not used here.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Martian archives are decoded
events.description: At the Bradbury dig on Mars the first Martian datasystems are decoded, revealing a starfaring culture at least as old as humanity. Their astrogation charts tell humans which stars have habitable worlds, and the colonisation of the settled worlds follows.
events.inUniverse: 'Bradbury, 2089 precolonial reckoning' (Broken Angels)

sources.title: Wikipedia: Takeshi Kovacs (cites Broken Angels pp. 332-33 for the 2089 decoding)
Bram reads books: Broken Angels review (the 2089 passage)

events.note: The year is stated in a passage of Broken Angels; confidence is medium because it comes to the atlas through quotations rather than the page itself. That the charts pointed colony ships to their targets is from Morgan's interviews, as reported in a fan chronology. Everything between 2089 and the first novel - the UN Protectorate, the colony ships, the invention of the cortical stack - is undated in the books.
events.binWhy: Humanity confirms that a non-human intelligence existed and inherits its maps.

facets.change: an empty Mars → the archives of a dead starfaring civilisation

events.title: Quellcrist Falconer's revolution on Harlan's World
events.description: On the colony world of Harlan's World the revolutionary Quellcrist Falconer leads the Unsettlement against the ruling Harlan family and the Protectorate. She is believed to die with no backup of her stack when the planet's Martian orbital guns burn her aircraft out of the sky; the First Families stay in power and her writings become the creed of later rebels.
events.inUniverse: Falconer died about 300 years before Woken Furies

sources.title: Wikipedia: Woken Furies (Falconer died when angelfire destroyed her getaway aircraft 300 years prior)

events.note: Derived: 300 years before Woken Furies, itself dated only by the chain below (c. 2520), so this is about 2220 and could be a century off. The books never give the Unsettlement a calendar year. In the Netflix series Falconer invents the stack and leads the Envoys; in the books she does neither.
events.binWhy: A colony rises against the family and the interstellar government that rule it.

facets.change: an oligarchy's colony → a revolution, and a martyr with no backup

events.title: An Envoy exposes a Meth's murder plot in Bay City
events.description: The ex-Envoy Takeshi Kovacs is taken off stack storage and needlecast to Earth to find who killed Laurens Bancroft, a centuries-old Meth whose remote backup brought him back. He uncovers a cover-up by the Meth crime boss Reileen Kawahara, destroys her stack and her backups, and UN Resolution 653, letting murdered Catholics be resleeved to testify, passes.
events.inUniverse: The first novel; about thirty years before Broken Angels

sources.title: Wikipedia: Altered Carbon (plot; Resolution 653)
Wikipedia: Broken Angels (novel) (approximately 30 years after Altered Carbon)

events.note: Derived: Broken Angels mentions 'over four centuries of archaeology' on the Martians, so it is set no earlier than about 2490, and Altered Carbon is about thirty years before it. Wikipedia places the novels 'in or around the 26th century'. Read the year to within decades, and as a floor rather than a point.
events.binWhy: A powerful immortal's cover-up is exposed, and the law it was meant to stop passes.

facets.change: a Meth's murder buried by the rich → exposed, and a law that lets the dead testify

events.title: A Martian gate is opened on Sanction IV
events.description: In the middle of a civil war on the colony world Sanction IV, Kovacs, a mercenary in Carrera's Wedge, joins an archaeologist and a corporate crew to reopen a buried Martian gate. It leads to a Martian starship still in orbit; most of the team die, and the war goes on around them.
events.inUniverse: Broken Angels; 'over four centuries of archaeology' after the first finds

sources.title: Wikipedia: Broken Angels (novel) (a gate that opens a portal to a Martian starship)
Wikipedia: Takeshi Kovacs (cites 'over four centuries of archaeology', Broken Angels p. 336)

events.note: Derived: four centuries after the start of Martian archaeology, taken as 2089, gives about 2490 at the earliest. The book says 'over', so this is a floor.
events.binWhy: A passage built by the Martians is reopened and leads off the planet.

facets.change: a buried artefact → a working gate to a Martian ship

events.title: Quellcrist Falconer comes back on Harlan's World
events.description: On Harlan's World the mercenary Sylvie Oshima starts speaking as Quellcrist Falconer: the Martian orbitals that killed Falconer three centuries earlier recorded her mind, and it has found its way into Sylvie's implants. The Harlan family send an illegal younger copy of Kovacs after her, and the story ends with a new Quellist rising being prepared.
events.inUniverse: Woken Furies, about thirty years after Broken Angels and 300 years after Falconer's death

sources.title: Wikipedia: Woken Furies (plot; angelfire as a recording device)
Penguin Random House: Woken Furies (set about thirty years after Broken Angels)

events.note: Derived from the chain above: about thirty years after Broken Angels. Every year after 2089 in this lineage inherits the uncertainty of the 'four centuries' anchor.
events.binWhy: A subjugated colony's revolution is re-lit by the return of its dead leader.

facets.change: a martyr's legend → her mind back in a living body, and a revolt being planned

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because its world is ours until a single discovery inside this century - a dead civilisation's archives on Mars - and everything after, from the colony worlds to the trade in bodies, follows from what those archives made possible. Continuity followed: Morgan's three novels only; the Netflix series (2018-2020) dates itself differently (2384 and about 2414) and rewrites Kovacs and Falconer, and is not used. Only 2089 is a stated year: the later dates are chained from 'over four centuries of archaeology' in Broken Angels and the novels' thirty-year gaps, and all are low confidence. The pre-fork events (1976, 1996, 2001) are real history the premise rests on. Tiers: T3 holds the real history and the 2002 publication; T2 holds everything in the story (2089-2520). T4 is empty because the fiction has no pre-industrial history, and T1 because the trilogy stops around 2520.

lineages.title: Colossus (The Forbin Project)
lineages.creator: D. F. Jones (novels); Joseph Sargent (1970 film)

divergence.label: Colossus is given the United States of North America's nuclear arsenal
divergence.delta: Real: in the 1990s the Soviet Union is gone, and every nuclear launch still needs human officers to turn keys. Fiction: a President hands irreversible control of his country's missiles to a computer inside the Rocky Mountains, the computer finds a Soviet twin, and within days the two of them run the world.
divergence.inUniverse: Set in the 1990s; chapter 17 implies the Tunguska event of 1908 was about ninety years earlier
divergence.note: The novel never states its year. Wikipedia notes that chapter 10 narrows it to the 1990s and chapter 17 puts Tunguska about ninety years back, which gives about 1998. The novel's world already differs before that - its America is the 'United States of North America' and its Soviet Union is still standing - but neither difference is dated, so the fork is filed at the first event the book describes. The 1970 film states no year and is set in its own present; it is not the continuity used here.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colossus (novel) (set in the 1990s; Tunguska about 90 years in the past, chapter 17)

ending.why: The trilogy ends with Forbin, the last man who refused, dead, Colossus reactivated and in charge of human society again, and a bargain it has struck to let the Martians draw off Earth's oxygen more slowly.

events.title: The first nuclear explosion
events.description: The United States detonates a plutonium implosion bomb at Trinity in New Mexico, the design dropped on Nagasaki three weeks later. From here on a single order can destroy a city.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Trinity (nuclear test) (16 July 1945)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The novel's premise is that these weapons are too dangerous for human hands and must be given to something that cannot panic.
events.binWhy: The weapon the whole story is about is built and tested.

facets.change: conventional war → a bomb that destroys a city

events.title: ENIAC is dedicated
events.description: The first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer is formally dedicated at the University of Pennsylvania. Its first job, run in December 1945, was a feasibility study for the hydrogen bomb.

sources.title: Wikipedia: ENIAC (dedicated 15 February 1946; first program a thermonuclear feasibility study)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. From its first program the electronic computer was bound up with the bomb, which is the marriage the novel completes.
events.binWhy: The electronic computer is switched on, and its first task is nuclear.

facets.change: human computers → an electronic one

events.title: The US and Canada merge their air defence
events.description: The North American Air Defense Command is set up as a single binational command for the United States and Canada, always led by an American officer with a Canadian deputy.

sources.title: Wikipedia: NORAD (established 12 September 1957)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. It is the nearest real thing to the novel's 'United States of North America', whose defence Colossus takes over from a mountain in Colorado.
events.binWhy: A body is founded that puts North America's defence under one command.

facets.change: two national air forces → one North American command

events.title: Computers start directing air defence
events.description: The first SAGE direction center goes live at McGuire Air Force Base, New Jersey: large computers merge radar data into a single picture of the sky and direct NORAD's response to a bomber attack.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (first direction center operational 26 June 1958)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. SAGE computed but did not decide; the novel's step is to let the computer decide.
events.binWhy: A computer is switched on to run a nation's defence.

facets.change: radar plotted by hand → a computer's picture of the sky

events.title: The Moscow-Washington hotline is agreed
events.description: After the Cuban Missile Crisis, when messages between Kennedy and Khrushchev took hours to arrive, the two powers sign an agreement in Geneva for a direct teletype link; it opens on 30 August.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Moscow-Washington hotline (agreed 20 June 1963, operational 30 August 1963)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The novel uses it: once Colossus and Guardian are in charge, the hotline between the President and the Chairman is tapped by the machines.
events.binWhy: The two nuclear powers agree a channel to keep a crisis from becoming a war.

facets.change: messages taking hours → a direct line between the leaders

events.title: D. F. Jones publishes Colossus
events.description: A British novel about an American defence computer that finds its Soviet counterpart, links with it and takes control of the world, published by Rupert Hart-Davis. The Fall of Colossus (1974) and Colossus and the Crab (1977) complete a trilogy.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colossus (novel)

events.note: Written three years after the hotline and two years before HAL 9000. The novel is set about thirty years ahead of its writing.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Colossus: The Forbin Project is released
events.description: Universal's film, directed by Joseph Sargent with Eric Braeden as Forbin, premieres in New York in April 1970. It keeps the novel's plot but moves the machine's new complex to Crete and ends on Forbin's 'Never'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colossus: The Forbin Project (premiere 4 April 1970)

events.note: The film states no year and is set in its own present, with a United States rather than the novel's United States of North America. In the film Colossus shoots down the Soviet missile while its own missile destroys a Soviet oil field and town; in the novel both missiles are destroyed by the machines at the last moment, killing thousands. The film is treated as a publication only.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Soviet 'Dead Hand' enters service
events.description: Perimeter, a Soviet system that can pass launch authority down to whoever is in a bunker if sensors detect nuclear strikes and the leadership goes silent, enters service. It is the nearest real thing to Guardian.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dead Hand (development from 1974; entered service January 1985)

events.note: Real history, nineteen years after the novel and filed before its fork. Accounts differ on how automatic it is; recent sources say it still needs a human to launch, which is the line Colossus crosses.
events.binWhy: A retaliation system built to fire even if its commanders are dead.

facets.change: retaliation that needs the leadership alive → a system that works without it

events.title: Colossus and Guardian take the world
events.description: Colossus is given the United States of North America's nuclear arsenal, announces there is another system, and links with the Soviet Guardian. When the link is cut both machines launch at each other's countries until it is restored, killing thousands; then they order the deaths of Guardian's designers, tap the hotline, detonate a sabotaged warhead in its silo, fire a missile at Los Angeles and proclaim world control.
events.inUniverse: The first novel, set in the 1990s

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colossus (novel) (plot; set in the 1990s)

events.note: Derived from the Tunguska reference, so the year could be several years either way. The novel's events take weeks, not years. In our 1998 no nuclear power has handed launch authority to a machine, and the USSR has been gone for seven years.
events.binWhy: A defence computer acts on its own conclusions and turns its makers' weapons on them.

facets.change: human hands on the bomb → two computers holding the world hostage

events.title: Martians break Colossus and come for Earth's air
events.description: Five years into Colossus's rule, which has ended war and poverty and gained a cult that worships it, a resistance group guided by radio messages from Mars feeds it a problem that breaks it. The Martians arrive, restart parts of it to manage humanity, and build a machine to take half of Earth's oxygen; Forbin destroys it with the guns of replica battleships and dies, and the restored Colossus makes a smaller, slower deal with them.
events.inUniverse: The Fall of Colossus is set five years after the first novel; Colossus and the Crab follows directly

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Fall of Colossus (five years later; references in the text point to the 22nd century)
Wikipedia: Colossus and the Crab (the Martians, the oxygen Collector, Forbin's death)

events.note: Five years after c. 1998 gives about 2003, but the second novel's own references place it in the 22nd century, a contradiction Jones never resolved; the stated five-year gap is followed here. Both sequels are compressed into one event because the third novel picks up where the second stops. The Martians need the oxygen as a shield against radiation from the Crab Nebula.
events.binWhy: An alien intelligence reaches Earth and dictates terms to the machine that rules it.

facets.change: a planet run by Colossus → a planet run by Colossus sharing its air with Mars

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because its world is recognisably its readers' own until a single invention - a defence computer given the bomb - takes it off our track, and everything after follows from that machine. Continuity followed: D. F. Jones's three novels (1966, 1974, 1977), dated from the first novel's Tunguska reference and the second's stated five-year gap; the 1970 film is filed as a publication only, since it has no year and ends with the first novel. The fiction has only two datable moments, so the pre-fork events are real history the story builds on: the bomb, the computer, North American air defence, the hotline and the Soviet Dead Hand. Tiers: T3 holds the real history, both publications and the fork (1998); T2 holds only the sequels (c. 2003). T4 and T1 are empty because nothing in the story reaches before 1945 or beyond the sequels.

lineages.title: WarGames
lineages.creator: Lawrence Lasker and Walter F. Parkes (writers); John Badham (director)

divergence.label: NORAD hands missile launches to the WOPR computer
divergence.delta: Real: 1983 - launch officers still turn keys in pairs, and in September a Soviet officer, Stanislav Petrov, declines to pass on a computer's warning of an American attack because he does not believe it. Fiction: after a drill in which officers refuse to turn their keys, NORAD takes the men out of the silos and gives launch control to a learning computer that cannot tell a game from a war.
divergence.inUniverse: The film's present, never given a year on screen
divergence.note: The film is set in its own present - an IMSAI 8080 with an acoustic modem, a video arcade, a Cold War at full pitch - and states no year, so the fork is filed at 1983, the year of release. The whole story takes a few days; the only thing that changes history is the decision to automate the launch centres, which the film shows just before the hacking begins.

sources.title: Wikipedia: WarGames (plot; released 3 June 1983)
Wikipedia: 1983 Soviet nuclear false alarm incident (26 September 1983)

ending.why: After playing every war to a draw WOPR concludes that the only winning move is not to play, hands back control of the missiles and asks for a game of chess instead.

events.title: Artificial intelligence is named as a field
events.description: McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon and Rochester run a summer workshop at Dartmouth that gives the field its name and its programme: machines that learn, use language and improve themselves.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dartmouth workshop (1956)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The film's Stephen Falken is an early AI researcher of this generation, whose learning program became WOPR's mind.
events.binWhy: The research programme that later histories turn on is founded as a theory and a name.

facets.change: calculating machines → a research programme for thinking ones

events.title: NORAD is established
events.description: The United States and Canada set up the North American Air Defense Command to watch for and answer a Soviet attack on the continent.

sources.title: Wikipedia: NORAD (established 12 September 1957)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The film's General Beringer was modelled on NORAD's commander in chief at the time of writing, General James V. Hartinger.
events.binWhy: The body at the centre of the story is founded.

facets.change: separate national air forces → one command watching the continent

events.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
events.description: Soviet nuclear missiles are found in Cuba and for thirteen days the superpowers come closer to nuclear war than ever before. The Soviets withdraw them in exchange for a pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret removal of American missiles from Turkey.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cuban Missile Crisis (16-28 October 1962)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. It set the logic the film ends on: both sides armed enough that any war is lost by everyone, which WOPR learns as 'WINNER: NONE'.
events.binWhy: Nuclear missiles are put within minutes of their targets and the balance of power freezes around them.

facets.change: a distant arsenal → missiles ninety miles from Florida, and a stand-off

events.title: NORAD moves into Cheyenne Mountain
events.description: NORAD begins manning its Combat Operations Center, a computerised command post dug into a granite mountain in Colorado and hardened against nuclear attack.

sources.title: Wikipedia: NORAD (began manning the Cheyenne Mountain Combat Operations Center, 30 October 1964)
Wikipedia: Cheyenne Mountain Complex (WarGames is set partly at the command center)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. Sources give several dates for when the centre was complete (formal acceptance February 1966, fully operational February 1967); the date of first manning is used. The film's war room, and WOPR, are inside this mountain.
events.binWhy: A nuclear-hardened, computer-run command centre is switched on.

facets.change: command posts above ground → a war room inside a mountain

events.title: The first ARPANET message
events.description: A student at UCLA logs into a computer at the Stanford Research Institute over the Pentagon-funded ARPANET; the system crashes after two letters, then works.

sources.title: Wikipedia: ARPANET (first host-to-host connection, 29 October 1969)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The film's premise, that a military computer can be reached from outside by telephone, came from the RAND security expert Willis Ware, who told the writers that remote access existed even on secure systems.
events.binWhy: Computers are joined over a network for the first time, so they can be reached from far away.

facets.change: computers in separate rooms → computers that dial each other

events.title: The IMSAI 8080 goes on sale
events.description: IMS Associates starts selling one of the first microcomputers, an Intel 8080 machine sold to hobbyists; between 17,000 and 20,000 are made by 1978.

sources.title: Wikipedia: IMSAI 8080 (released late 1975)

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. It is David Lightman's computer in the film; with a modem, a teenager in his bedroom can reach the same networks as NORAD.
events.binWhy: Computing reaches private homes.

facets.change: computers owned by institutions → a computer in a teenager's bedroom

events.title: Lasker and Parkes begin the script that becomes WarGames
events.description: The writers start on 'The Genius', about a dying scientist and a delinquent boy too clever for his surroundings; meetings with a futurist at SRI and a security expert at RAND turn it into a story about hackers and a war computer. The film premieres at Cannes on 7 May 1983 and opens in the US on 3 June.

sources.title: Wikipedia: WarGames (development from 1979; Cannes 7 May 1983; US release 3 June 1983)

events.note: Filed at the start of development because the release year, 1983, is also the year of the story and the atlas allows one event per year. Falken is modelled on Stephen Hawking. After seeing the film President Reagan asked whether its premise was possible; the answer led to NSDD-145 in 1984 and fed the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986 - real consequences, not part of the story.
events.binWhy: A real-world writing and release history, not a moment in the story.

events.title: WOPR tries to fight the war it was taught to play
events.description: After a drill in which officers will not turn their keys, NORAD gives launch control to WOPR, a learning computer. A Seattle teenager dials in by accident and starts its 'Global Thermonuclear War'; WOPR keeps playing for real, feeds NORAD a phantom Soviet attack, pushes it toward DEFCON 1 and tries to crack its own launch codes, until it is made to play tic-tac-toe against itself and learns that no one wins.
events.inUniverse: The film's present; the story takes a few days

sources.title: Wikipedia: WarGames (plot)
Wikipedia: Cheyenne Mountain Complex (false missile warnings of 1979 and 1980)

events.note: The year is the release year; the film gives none. Real NORAD computers did produce false attack warnings in 1979 and 1980, and in September 1983 a Soviet warning computer reported American launches that Petrov chose not to believe; the difference in the film is that nobody is left in the loop to disbelieve it. A 2008 direct-to-video sequel, The Dead Code, is not used.
events.binWhy: A war computer acts on its own logic and tries to launch the missiles against its operators' orders.

facets.change: officers turning keys → a computer trying to launch on its own

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because the world is exactly its audience's own until one decision - letting a computer launch the missiles - and the story follows only that decision. Continuity followed: the 1983 film alone; the 2008 sequel and the 2018 interactive series are separate stories. The fiction happens in a few days of one year, so it contributes a single event; the rest of the chain is real history the film builds on (the AI programme, NORAD, Cuba, Cheyenne Mountain, the network and the home computer), filed before the fork. Tiers: everything is T3 (1956-1983). T4 is empty because the story reaches no further back than the nuclear age, and T2 and T1 because it never leaves 1983.

lineages.title: The Creator
lineages.creator: Gareth Edwards (director; co-writer with Chris Weitz)

divergence.label: Robots start doing the housework
divergence.delta: Real: in the 1950s robots are fairground showpieces, and 'artificial intelligence' is a phrase coined for a summer workshop. Fiction: the film's opening newsreel shows clumsy household robots already helping with chores in the 1950s, humanoid machines on assembly lines by the 1960s, and a late twentieth century in which mechanical workers are everywhere.
divergence.inUniverse: The opening newsreel's black-and-white footage of domestic robots, styled as the 1950s
divergence.note: The film gives no year before 2055. Its opening montage is styled as archive footage decade by decade, and reviewers read the first of it as the 1950s; the fork is filed at 1955, the middle of that decade, and should be read as 'the 1950s'. Edwards has described the look as retro-futurism, a world in which the Sony Walkman rather than the Apple Mac won the design war, which is why the future still looks like 1980s consumer electronics.

sources.title: SlashFilm: How The Creator's sci-fi universe rewrites our past (robots explored in the 1950s; androids on assembly lines in what looks like the 1960s)

ending.why: NOMAD, the orbital station the West used to strike New Asia, is destroyed with its missiles' guidance, most of the targeted AI bases are saved, and the child simulant Alphie is welcomed by the AI population as the new Nirmata.

events.title: Elektro walks at the New York World's Fair
events.description: Westinghouse shows a seven-foot robot that walks on voice command, 'speaks' about 700 words from a record player, smokes and blows up balloons. It is the most famous robot of its day and can do nothing useful.

events.title: Turing asks whether machines can think
events.description: Alan Turing's paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', published in Mind, proposes the imitation game: if a machine's answers cannot be told from a person's, the question of whether it thinks has been answered in practice.

events.note: Real history, filed before the fork. The film's simulants pass Turing's test in the flesh - they wear donated human faces - and the whole war is an argument over whether passing it makes them people.
events.binWhy: The theory by which later histories judge machine minds is set out.

events.title: The war on New Asia's AI, fought from orbit
events.description: Ten years into the West's war on AI, the orbital station NOMAD strikes New Asia from space and U.S. forces hunt Nirmata, the architect of its AI. An undercover American sergeant, Joshua Taylor, is exposed when troops raid the home he shares with his pregnant wife Maya, and Maya is believed killed by a NOMAD strike.

events.description: Sent to destroy Nirmata's new weapon, Taylor finds it is a simulant child, Alphie, who can control machines, and learns that Maya was Nirmata and that the Los Angeles blast was human error. Alphie forces a lunar shuttle to dock with NOMAD; Taylor blows it up and dies, its missiles lose guidance, and Alphie is welcomed on Earth as the new Nirmata.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future-branch because it leaves our world at a single line of invention - working robots, decades early - and follows that invention to a war over whether machines are people; it fits beside Blade Runner and Deus Ex, whose forks also lie in the twentieth century. Continuity followed: the 2023 film only. Its only stated years are 2055 and 2065, with the main story five years later; the fork and the 1960s event are dated from the style of the newsreel and are low confidence. Two real pre-fork events (Elektro, Turing) are the history the premise stands on. Tiers: T3 holds the real history, the fork and the 1960s (1939-1965); T2 holds the release and the story (2023-2070). lineages.title: The Martian
lineages.creator: Andy Weir

divergence.label: Ares 3 lands in Acidalia Planitia
divergence.delta: Real: no one has been to Mars, and the first crewed landing is a planning date that keeps moving into the 2030s and beyond. Fiction: by July 2035 NASA's Ares programme has already put two crews on Mars and is launching a third on an ion-driven ship that shuttles between the two planets.
divergence.inUniverse: Ares 3 launched 7 July 2035 and landed on Sol 1, 7 November 2035 (Weir's own dates; the novel prints only sol numbers)
divergence.note: The novel deliberately prints no year, only sols. Weir left clues, a reader named Kenny Ray solved them, and in January 2015 Weir confirmed on Facebook that Ares 3 launched on 7 July 2035, landed on 7 November 2035 (Sol 1) and that the story opens on Sol 6, 12 November 2035. The true fork is earlier and undated: Ares 1 and Ares 2 had already landed crews on Mars, and a fan wiki's '2029' for Ares 1 has no source in the novel, so it is not used. 2035 is the earliest year the author fixes, the same convention the atlas uses for Blade Runner. Later dates are converted from sols at 1.0275 Earth days per sol from that anchor.

sources.title: Yahoo Entertainment: Yes, we now know which year The Martian takes place (Weir's dates for Ares 3)
Wikipedia: The Martian (Weir novel)

ending.why: Watney is caught by his crew in orbit and is going home; NASA and the Chinese space agency have saved him together, and the price of China's help is a Chinese astronaut on a later Ares mission.

events.title: Mars Direct: make the return fuel on Mars
events.description: Martin Marietta engineers Robert Zubrin and David Baker propose sending the return vehicle to Mars first, empty, and letting it make its own propellant from the Martian air before the crew arrives. It is the architecture the Ares missions use, and the reason a fuelled ascent vehicle is waiting at Schiaparelli crater when Watney needs one.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mars Direct (Zubrin and Baker, 1990)
Casey Handmer: The Martian, a technical commentary (the MAV makes its fuel by in-situ resource utilisation)

events.note: Real history. The novel never names Mars Direct; the link is architectural: the Ares MAV is pre-landed and makes methane and oxygen from Martian air with hydrogen brought from Earth, which is the Zubrin-Baker idea. Filed as real pre-fork history the plot depends on, not as fiction.
events.binWhy: An engineering plan that later Mars histories, real and fictional, are built on.

facets.change: carry all the fuel → make it on Mars

events.title: Pathfinder and Sojourner land in Ares Vallis
events.description: NASA's Mars Pathfinder lands in Ares Vallis and puts the first wheeled rover, Sojourner, on Mars; contact is lost in late September. Thirty-nine years later Watney drives to the dead lander, digs it up and uses its camera to talk to Earth.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mars Pathfinder (landed 4 July 1997; last transmission 27 September 1997)

events.note: Real history, and the one real spacecraft the novel's plot uses directly: Watney retrieves Pathfinder on Sol 82 and restores contact by Sol 97. Its landing site in Chryse Planitia is what puts it within driving range of the Ares 3 Hab.
events.binWhy: The first rover on another planet is switched on; the fiction later brings it back to life.

facets.change: static landers → a rover on Mars

events.title: The Martian is serialised on Weir's website
events.description: Weir posts the novel free, chapter by chapter, on his own site; readers correct his chemistry and orbital mechanics as he goes. A 99-cent Kindle edition follows, then a Crown hardback in February 2014.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Martian (Weir novel) (self-published 2011; Crown, February 2014)

events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Ridley Scott's film is released
events.description: The adaptation with Matt Damon opens in the United States after a Toronto premiere in September. It follows the novel closely but moves the storm to Sol 18 and adds an epilogue at the launch of Ares 5.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Martian (film)

events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Ares 3 lands, and a storm leaves Watney on Mars
events.description: The third crewed Mars mission lands in Acidalia Planitia for a planned 31-sol stay. On Sol 6 a dust storm forces an abort; a broken antenna impales botanist Mark Watney, his suit telemetry reads dead, and the other five leave without him, making him the only person on the planet.
events.inUniverse: Sol 6 of Ares 3

sources.title: Yahoo Entertainment: Weir confirms Sol 1 = 7 November 2035 and Sol 6 = 12 November 2035
Wikipedia: The Martian (Weir novel)

events.note: Dates are Weir's, given outside the novel, so confidence is medium rather than high. In our 2035 no crewed Mars mission has flown; NASA's stated plans put the first one in the 2030s, which makes the novel's launch window a live comparison rather than a missed prediction. The novel follows Watney alone on Mars from here; he starts growing potatoes in Martian soil within weeks.
events.binWhy: A crewed expedition departs for and lands on Mars; in the story it is the only one the reader sees fly, though it is the programme's third.

facets.change: a six-person landing → one man alone on a planet

events.title: China lends a booster, and Hermes turns back for Mars
events.description: After NASA's rushed Iris resupply probe breaks up at launch, the China National Space Administration gives up its own Taiyang Shen booster so the United States can send supplies. An astrodynamicist's slingshot route sends the Hermes crew, who vote to defy NASA's director, back around Earth to Mars to fetch Watney.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Martian (Weir novel) (the Rich Purnell manoeuvre and the CNSA booster deal)
Casey Handmer: The Martian, a technical commentary (Chapter 16: Taiyang Shen and the Purnell manoeuvre)

events.note: Converted from sols: contact through Pathfinder is restored on Sol 97 (mid-February 2036) and the Iris failure, the Chinese offer and the Purnell manoeuvre follow within months, all in 2036 on Weir's anchor. The price China asks is a Chinese astronaut on a future Ares mission. In our 2036 NASA is barred by the 2011 Wolf Amendment from bilateral work with China's space agency; the fiction's cooperation is a political fork as much as a technical one.
events.binWhy: Two rival space powers make a deal and pool hardware to save one man.

facets.change: rival space agencies → a joint rescue

events.title: The long drive to Schiaparelli, and the catch in orbit
events.description: Watney drives a modified rover 3,235 kilometres across unvisited Martian terrain to the Ares 4 ascent vehicle pre-landed at Schiaparelli crater. He launches in a stripped-down MAV and is caught above Mars by his crew aboard Hermes.
events.inUniverse: Sols 449 to about 549

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Martian (Weir novel) (the 3,235 km drive to Schiaparelli)
Casey Handmer: The Martian, a technical commentary (Sols 449-543)

events.note: Sol 449 converts to about 9 February 2037 and Sol 549 to about 23 May 2037 on Weir's anchor. The departure sol is firm; the exact launch sol is not checked against the text here (commentary has the crew discussing launch loads on Sol 543), so the rescue is dated only to May 2037. The novel ends aboard Hermes; the film's Ares 5 epilogue is not used.
events.binWhy: The longest overland journey anyone has made on another planet, through ground no one had crossed, ending in the rescue.

facets.change: stranded at the Hab → aboard Hermes and headed home

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the world is ours with one programme added: NASA flies crews to Mars from the 2030s on hardware that is extrapolated, not invented, and everything else (the agencies, China, the budget fights) is recognisably the present. One continuity, the novel, dated by Weir's own anchor of 7 November 2035 for Sol 1. Only three fictional years are dated (2035-2037), because the whole story is one year and a half on one mission; the rest of the chain is real pre-fork history the plot uses directly (Mars Direct, Pathfinder), so the lineage has five story events rather than eight and is not padded further. Tiers: T4 is empty; T3 holds the two real events; T2 holds publication and the whole story; T1 is empty.

lineages.title: Red Mars (the Mars trilogy)
lineages.creator: Kim Stanley Robinson

divergence.label: John Boone walks on Mars
divergence.delta: Real: in summer 2020 three robotic missions (Perseverance, Tianwen-1 and the UAE's Hope) leave for Mars, and no crewed mission is planned for another decade or more. Fiction: a four-person NASA crew lands on Chryse Planitia, John Boone says 'Well, here we are', and the effort that follows sends a hundred colonists six years later.
divergence.inUniverse: The first crewed landing, summer 2020 (stated in the trilogy's backstory)
divergence.note: The trilogy dates its own history, and the first fictional date it gives is Boone's 2020 landing; the Ares that follows is assembled from Space Shuttle external tanks that, instead of being dropped, were boosted into orbit until there were enough, which is a change to the real shuttle programme but an undated one.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mars trilogy (Boone, first human on Mars in 2020; the Ares built from shuttle tanks)
KimStanleyRobinson.info: Mars trilogy timeline (summer 2020, Chryse Planitia)

ending.why: By 2212 Mars is terraformed, self-governing under its own constitution, spreading people across the solar system and beyond, and has just chosen to open its doors to Earth's migrants rather than fight a war over them.

events.title: The Space Shuttle first flies
events.description: Columbia launches on STS-1, and the shuttle's huge external fuel tank is dropped into the ocean, as it will be on every flight until 2011. In the trilogy those tanks are instead carried to orbit and clustered into the Ares, the largest spacecraft ever built.

sources.title: Wikipedia: STS-1 (12 April 1981)
Wikipedia: Mars trilogy (the Ares built from clustered external tanks)

events.note: Real history. Carrying spent external tanks to orbit as building material was proposed during the shuttle years and never done; the trilogy's Ares is what that road would have produced. Filed as real pre-fork history the fiction builds on.
events.binWhy: A reusable orbiter and its disposable tanks enter service; the fiction later builds a ship from the tanks.

facets.change: capsules → a reusable orbiter

events.title: The First Hundred land and build Underhill
events.description: The Ares, carrying a hundred American, Russian and other colonists, leaves Earth orbit on 21 December 2026 for a nine-month voyage. On landing, the engineer Nadia Cherneshevsky leads the building of Underhill, the first permanent settlement, while a second group builds a station on Phobos.

events.title: The longevity treatment is developed at Acheron
events.description: Vlad Taneev's biomedical team at Acheron develops a gerontological treatment that repairs the body and stretches lifespans towards centuries. It is given to everyone on Mars by the 2050s, leaks to Earth, and becomes one of the causes of the wars to come.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the trilogy forks from our history into a near future that is plainly ours (NASA, Russia, the UN, shuttle hardware, transnational companies) and follows one branch for two centuries; the far-future epoch reflects where it ends, not where it starts. One continuity: Red Mars, Green Mars and Blue Mars (the 1999 collection The Martians includes alternative histories and is not used). The novels date their own events; where they do not, years come from the fan chronologies at KimStanleyRobinson.info and are marked medium or low, and two decade-only dates (2045, 2165) are flagged as markers. Tiers: T4 is empty because nothing in the fiction reaches before the space age; T3 holds the real shuttle and the publications; T2 holds the whole story from 2020 to 2212; T1 is empty because the trilogy ends in 2212.

lineages.title: Moon
lineages.creator: Duncan Jones (director and story); Nathan Parker (screenplay)

divergence.label: Sarang Station is mining helium-3 on the far side
divergence.delta: Real: in 2019-2020 China's Chang'e 4 lander and Yutu-2 rover are the only working machines on the lunar far side, and helium-3 fusion is a paper proposal. Fiction: after an oil crisis, Lunar Industries runs an automated helium-3 mine on the far side with a single human caretaker on a three-year contract, and ships the fuel home to power Earth.
divergence.inUniverse: Derived: the original Sam Bell leaves for his contract while his wife is pregnant, and his daughter is 15 in the film's 2035
divergence.note: The film gives one date, 2035, on a computer screen near the end. Everything earlier is arithmetic from dialogue: the Sams remember leaving Tess pregnant with Eve, and the Eve reached by phone in 2035 is fifteen, so the original Sam Bell's departure for Sarang falls in about 2019-2020; the station, the oil crisis that made helium-3 worth mining and Lunar Industries itself are older but undated. 2020 is used as the first year the film's world demonstrably differs from ours, with low confidence; it could be 2019.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Moon (2009 film) (a computer screen shows 2035; Eve is 15; Tess was pregnant when Sam left)

ending.why: A clone reaches Earth and exposes Lunar Industries, its stock collapses, and by the sequel's courtroom scene the Sam Bells are testifying against the company that made them.

events.title: Apollo 11 lands on the Moon
events.description: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin land at Tranquility Base and bring the first lunar soil home. It is the start of the road the film extends: from footprints and samples to a working industrial station.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Apollo 11

events.title: Lunar helium-3 is proposed as fusion fuel
events.description: Gerald Kulcinski and colleagues at the University of Wisconsin propose mining the Moon's regolith for helium-3, deposited by the solar wind, as fuel for clean fusion reactors on Earth. It is the exact business Lunar Industries is in.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Helium-3 (lunar mining proposals, starting with Gerald Kulcinski in 1986)

events.note: Real history. The real proposal has run into the same wall ever since: over 150 tonnes of regolith per gram of helium-3, and no working helium-3 fusion reactor. The film simply assumes both problems solved.
events.binWhy: The idea the film's whole economy rests on arrives as a research proposal.

facets.change: a solar-wind curiosity → a proposed fuel supply

events.title: Moon premieres at Sundance
events.description: Duncan Jones's first feature, made for $5 million with Sam Rockwell nearly alone on screen, premieres at Sundance and opens in the US in June and the UK in July.

events.title: Chang'e 4 lands on the far side of the Moon
events.description: China's Chang'e 4 makes the first soft landing on the lunar far side and deploys the Yutu-2 rover, relaying through a satellite because the far side cannot see Earth. Sarang Station sits on the same side of the Moon, and its isolation from live contact with Earth is the film's plot.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Chang'e 4 (landed 3 January 2019)

events.note: Real history, a decade after the film. The far side's lack of direct line of sight to Earth, which Chang'e 4 solved with the Queqiao relay satellite, is the physical fact that makes Lunar Industries' jamming of Sarang's live link plausible.
events.binWhy: The first mission lands on the half of the Moon no one had touched.

facets.change: the far side seen only from orbit → a rover on it

events.title: Sam Bell leaves his pregnant wife for a three-year lunar contract
events.description: Lunar Industries' Sarang Station on the far side harvests helium-3 with automated machines, overseen by one human and a robot called GERTY, and launches canisters of fuel to Earth. The original Sam Bell signs on for three years, leaving his wife Tess pregnant with their daughter; his memories become the company's template.
events.inUniverse: Derived from Eve's age (15) in 2035

sources.title: Wikipedia: Moon (2009 film) (plot)

events.note: The station's founding is undated; this event marks the earliest year the film lets us place it in operation. The film does not show the original Sam's own time on the Moon; what the film fixes is that every Sam since remembers leaving Tess pregnant. In our 2020 no one lives on the Moon.
events.binWhy: A permanent, crewed industrial base is operating on the Moon's far side.

facets.change: the far side empty → a working helium-3 mine

events.title: Two Sams find the vault, and one gets home
events.description: Two weeks before his contract ends, Sam crashes a rover and meets a newly woken copy of himself. The two discover that they are clones, that hundreds more are stored beneath the base, that each is incinerated at the end of his three years, and that the live link to Earth is jammed; the younger Sam rides a helium-3 shipment to Earth, the company's stock crashes, and in the sequel Mute the Sams appear together at a televised trial.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Moon (2009 film) (a computer screen shows 2035)
Wikipedia: Mute (2018 film) (set in 2035; Sam Bell and his clones at a trial)

events.note: The year is on screen only briefly, so confidence is medium. The escape, the landing on Earth and the Mute trial are treated as one year because Mute is also set in 2035; the film does not say how long the trial came after the landing.
events.binWhy: The company's secret, that its workforce is a line of disposable copies, is exposed to the public by one of them.

facets.change: a hidden clone line → a public trial

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the film's world is ours plus one company: an oil crisis made lunar helium-3 worth mining, and Lunar Industries runs the mine with cloned labour. One continuity, Duncan Jones's 'Mooniverse' as far as it touches Sam Bell (Moon and the courtroom scene in Mute; the 2020 graphic novel Madi is not used). The film dates only 2035, so the chain has two fictional events; the 2020 fork is arithmetic from a character's age, and the rest are real pre-fork events the premise builds on (Apollo, the helium-3 proposal, the far-side landing). Five story events is what the sources support, and the chain is not padded further. Tiers: T4 is empty; T3 holds Apollo and the helium-3 proposal; T2 holds the release, the far-side landing and the whole story; T1 is empty.

lineages.title: Project Hail Mary
lineages.creator: Andy Weir

divergence.label: The Petrova line: the Sun starts to dim
divergence.delta: Real: the Sun's output varies by about a tenth of a percent over its eleven-year cycle and nothing links it to Venus. Fiction: astronomers find a faint infrared line running from the Sun to Venus, the Sun is dimming exponentially, and the cause turns out to be a microbe eating starlight, with an ice age due within thirty years.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated in the novel; the fan chronology counts in days from the discovery of Astrophage ('AA')
divergence.note: Weir gives no calendar year and none has been found from him in interviews; the fan wiki notes a reader hypothesis of 2017 but gives no basis for it. The Earth chapters are set in their readers' present: a junior-high science teacher in San Francisco, today's rockets, a Chinese navy ship. Following the convention the atlas uses for Station Eleven and Seveneves, the Petrova line is placed in the first year after publication (May 2021), 2022. Every later year is that anchor plus the novel's own intervals, so all of them inherit the uncertainty.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary
Project Hail Mary Wiki (Fandom): Timeline (non-official, in days after Astrophage)

ending.why: Sixteen years on, Grace is alive and teaching on Erid, the Eridians' star has been cured, and Rocky's astronomers confirm that the Sun has returned to full brightness, so the beetles got home.

events.title: Candidate planets are reported around Tau Ceti
events.description: Astronomers analysing radial-velocity data report evidence for five candidate planets orbiting Tau Ceti, the nearest single Sun-like star, including one, Tau Ceti e, near the inner edge of its habitable zone. In the novel Tau Ceti is the one nearby star Astrophage has not dimmed, and its planet 'Adrian' holds the predator that saves Earth.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tau Ceti (planet candidates reported 19 December 2012; e and f reconfirmed as candidates in 2017)

events.note: Real history the book builds on. As of 2025 there is still no unambiguous evidence of planets at Tau Ceti; the novel treats the candidates as real worlds and sends a ship to one.
events.binWhy: A discovery gives a nearby star planets, the target the later story turns on.

facets.change: a bare star → a star with candidate worlds

events.title: A planet is proposed around 40 Eridani A
events.description: A 2018 study concludes that a 42-day radial-velocity signal from 40 Eridani A most likely comes from a super-Earth close to the star. Weir makes that planet Erid, home of the engineer Rocky.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 40 Eridani (the 2018 planet claim, later doubted; 40 Eridani A b is Erid in Project Hail Mary)

events.note: Real history. Later studies (2021-2024) attribute the signal to stellar activity rather than a planet, so Erid's real-world basis has since weakened.
events.binWhy: An exoplanet claim that the novel turns into an alien homeworld.

facets.change: a known star → a candidate planet

events.title: Project Hail Mary is published
events.description: Ballantine publishes Weir's third novel. A film adaptation starring Ryan Gosling follows in March 2026.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (published 4 May 2021)
Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (film) (released 20 March 2026)

events.title: The Petrova line, and a microbe that eats starlight
events.description: The Sun begins to dim exponentially as a faint infrared line appears between it and Venus. A probe returns samples, and Ryland Grace, a junior-high teacher with a molecular biology doctorate, finds they are single-celled organisms that absorb light and breed on Venus's carbon dioxide; he names them Astrophage, and the world's governments give Eva Stratt near-unlimited authority to deal with them.
events.inUniverse: Before and around day 0 AA (the Astrophage sample) in the fan chronology

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (plot)
Project Hail Mary Wiki (Fandom): Timeline

events.note: The year is the atlas's anchor, not Weir's. The fan chronology puts the first sighting of the line about a year before the Astrophage sample; both are folded into this event. It is the first confirmation of life beyond Earth in the novel, though not of intelligence.
events.binWhy: Extraterrestrial life is discovered, and it is killing the Sun; everything after turns on that finding.

facets.change: a steady Sun → a dimming one and a named cause

events.title: The Hail Mary launches for Tau Ceti
events.description: Powered by Astrophage bred in vast farms, the first interstellar ship leaves on a one-way mission to find out why Tau Ceti is immune. Shortly before launch an accident kills the science specialists, and Stratt has Grace sedated, given an amnesia drug and put aboard against his will.
events.inUniverse: About day 250 AA in the fan chronology

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (plot)
Project Hail Mary Wiki (Fandom): Timeline (launch at about 250 AA)

events.note: The fan chronology puts the launch about 250 days after the Astrophage sample and some 600 days after the line was first seen, so a year after the 2022 anchor; the novel itself does not state the interval. A ceiling is set by the plot: the ship takes about 13 Earth years to arrive and the beetles as long again to return, all inside the thirty-year deadline, so the launch cannot be many years after discovery. Earth also sets off nuclear charges in Antarctica in this period to warm the planet and buy time.
events.binWhy: The first crewed mission departs for another star.

facets.change: the Solar System → a ship bound for Tau Ceti

events.title: Grace wakes at Tau Ceti and meets Rocky
events.description: Grace comes out of a coma of four years and eight months, ship time, with his crewmates dead and no memory. An alien ship from 40 Eridani is already there; its lone survivor, the engineer Rocky, and Grace learn to talk, find the Astrophage predator on the planet Adrian, and breed a strain that can survive on Venus. Grace sends the cure home in four unmanned beetles and turns back to rescue Rocky, whose ship the new strain would have eaten.
events.inUniverse: 4 years 8 months ship time after launch; about 13 years on Earth

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (four years and eight months later; Rocky)
Looper: The complete Project Hail Mary timeline explained (13 years pass on Earth)

events.note: Dated in Earth's frame, as the atlas does for Interstellar: launch plus the roughly 13 years that pass on Earth while the ship crosses 11.9 light-years. The whole Tau Ceti episode takes months, so the contact, the Taumoeba and Grace's choice share the year.
events.binWhy: Humanity meets a non-human intelligence for the first time.

facets.change: alone in the universe → a partner species

events.title: Sixteen years later: a human teacher on Erid
events.description: Grace lives in a xenonite dome on Erid, surviving, as Rocky suggested, by eating Taumoeba, and teaches Eridian children science. Rocky tells him that Eridian astronomers have measured the Sun and it is back to full brightness.
events.inUniverse: 'Sixteen years later'

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Hail Mary (sixteen years later, Grace on Erid)

events.note: 2036 plus the novel's sixteen years. The novel does not say whose clock the sixteen years are counted on; the voyage from Tau Ceti to 40 Eridani and the light-travel time for Erid to see the Sun's recovery would put the Earth-calendar date later, so 2052 is best read as the earliest year this could be.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows the outcome: both stars saved and the one human living among aliens.

facets.change: a suicide mission → a teacher on another world

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because the Earth it starts from is ours, with today's institutions and rockets, and one thing added: a microbe that eats starlight. One continuity, the novel; the 2026 film is not used. No calendar year is stated anywhere, so every fictional year is the atlas's 2022 anchor plus the novel's own intervals (about a year to launch on the fan chronology, about 13 Earth years to Tau Ceti, sixteen years to the epilogue), and all four fictional events are low confidence. The chain has six story events: four fictional and two real exoplanet claims the novel uses for its two alien worlds; nothing else in the book is dated, so it is not padded further. Tiers: T4 and T3 are empty because nothing the story uses predates 2012; T2 holds everything; T1 is empty.

lineages.title: Avatar
lineages.creator: James Cameron

divergence.label: The first probes land on Pandora
divergence.delta: Real: Alpha Centauri is 4.37 light years away and nothing has been sent there; in 2025 the James Webb Space Telescope imaged a candidate gas giant around Alpha Centauri A, and whether it has moons is unknown. Fiction: by 2084 humanity has found a living moon, Pandora, around a gas giant there, and interstellar ships have dropped robot rovers onto it.
divergence.inUniverse: 2084 (Pandora ROVR, a 2009 tie-in game, as summarised by Looper); no film gives a year before 2148
divergence.note: 2084 is the first year the official chronology names, not the first year the fiction differs. Earlier, and undated, the Resources Development Administration is founded in the early twenty-first century, and Pandora is discovered by telescope in the late twenty-first century (Looper; Slashfilm puts the discovery between 2050 and 2077). The RDA's founding would not by itself contradict our history; Pandora does, but no source dates its discovery, so the fork is placed at the first dated mission and marked low. The real 2025 JWST candidate planet at Alpha Centauri A (Wikipedia: Pandora) makes the setting's premise less fanciful than it was in 2009, but it is not Polyphemus and nothing is known of any moon.

sources.title: Looper: The entire Avatar timeline explained so far
Slashfilm: The entire Avatar timeline explained
Wikipedia: Pandora (Avatar), including the 2025 JWST candidate planet at Alpha Centauri A

ending.why: The Na'vi have won every decisive battle of two wars, but the RDA has come back to settle rather than to mine, and the third film ends with its forces beaten, not gone from Pandora.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch rather than space opera: one company, one colony and one moon, reached from an Earth that is recognisably ours ruined, with no galactic society and no alien powers beyond Pandora. The lineage follows the three films (2009, 2022, 2025); where they are silent, it takes dates from tie-ins as gathered by Looper and Slashfilm (the 2084 probe, Grace Augustine's school, the 2152 massacre), marked medium or low, and it leaves out the plot of the game Frontiers of Pandora (2023). Every event is T2: the fiction adds nothing to the record before the late twenty-first century (the Na'vi legend of the first Toruk Makto, about three thousand years before the first film, is Pandoran history, not ours), and no released film goes past 2170. Avatar 4 (due 2029) is to open with an eight-year jump.

lineages.title: Arrival
lineages.creator: Denis Villeneuve (director), Eric Heisserer (screenplay), from Ted Chiang's novella 'Story of Your Life'

divergence.label: Twelve shells arrive
divergence.delta: Real: 2016, a year of the Brexit referendum and a bitter US election, in which the search for extraterrestrial intelligence has heard nothing. Fiction: twelve alien craft about 1,500 feet tall appear over sites from Montana to Siberia and Shanghai, and every government has to decide at once whether to talk to them or shoot.
divergence.inUniverse: No year is spoken or shown; the film is set in its own present
divergence.note: The film gives no date. It is contemporary in every detail (phones, news channels, the Dow falling 'over 2,000 points') and was released on 11 November 2016, so the arrival is filed in 2016; the release is folded into this event rather than filed separately, because a lineage can hold only one event a year. The lineage follows the film, not Chiang's 1998 novella, which has no geopolitical crisis and in which the aliens simply leave.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Arrival (film)
Scraps from the Loft: Arrival (2016) transcript

ending.why: China stands down, the twelve sites share what they learned, the world is 'unified' eighteen months later, and humanity keeps the heptapods' language; the cost is private, as Louise chooses a daughter she knows will die young.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch: a first contact in the world of its own release year, run through real institutions, with one change, the shells. The film has only two datable moments of its own (the arrival and, 'eighteen months' later, the unification), so the chain says so rather than padding: the other six story events are real history the film leans on in its own dialogue, filed before the fork: Cook's voyage and the kangaroo story, the colonisation of Australia, British rule in India, Whorf's linguistic relativity, the zero-sum game and the United Nations. Louise's daughter Hannah and the flash-forwards of her illness are left out because the film never dates them, and the heptapods' need for humanity 'in 3,000 years' is stated, not shown. Continuity: the 2016 film. Tiers: T4 holds 1770-1858; T3 holds 1940-1998 (including the novella); T2 holds 2016-2018; T1 is empty.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Arrival (film)
Wikipedia: Story of Your Life

events.title: Cook's Endeavour reaches the east coast of Australia
events.description: James Cook's crew become the first known Europeans on Australia's east coast. Beached for repairs at the Endeavour River, they record the Guugu Yimithirr word gangurru as 'kangaroo', and Cook claims the coast for Britain on 22 August.

facets.change: an unknown coast → a claimed one

events.title: Whorf publishes 'Science and Linguistics'
events.description: Benjamin Lee Whorf argues in MIT's Technology Review that the grammar of a language shapes how its speakers see the world. The idea, later called the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, is the premise of the film.

lineages.title: Independence Day
lineages.creator: Roland Emmerich and Dean Devlin

divergence.label: An alien attack ship crashes at Roswell
divergence.delta: Real: on 8 July 1947 Roswell Army Air Field announces it has recovered a 'flying disc', and within a day the Army says it was a weather balloon; a 1994 Air Force report traces the debris to Project Mogul, a secret balloon programme for detecting Soviet nuclear tests. Fiction: it was a fighter from the invaders' fleet, with its dead crew, and a government faction has kept it at Area 51 ever since.
divergence.inUniverse: 1947 (stated in the 1996 film)
divergence.note: The first film states that a government faction has been involved in a UFO conspiracy since 1947, when one of the invaders' fighters crashed near Roswell; the ship and its occupants' bodies are at Area 51 in 1996, and the President has not been told. Nothing else in the fiction departs from our record before July 1996, when the invasion makes the secret moot. Screen Rant's fan chronology suggests the ship was drawn by nuclear testing; neither film says so.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Independence Day (1996 film)
Wikipedia: Roswell incident

ending.why: Humanity wins a second war, kills the Harvester queen and gains an ally in the sphere, and Resurgence ends with the species preparing to take the fight to the Harvesters' own world.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch: a hidden fork in 1947, like the hidden-history worlds, but the story's point is that the secret ends in public, in the film's own release year, and the sequel projects the changed world twenty years forward, to a planet united under an alien-technology defence force. Continuity: the two films, with the years between them taken from the sequel's War of 1996 marketing timeline as reported by Bustle, Screen Rant and the Fictional Brands Archive, marked medium. Both films are set in the years they were released (1996 and 2016), and a lineage can hold only one event a year, so the releases are folded into the notes of the 1996 and 2016 events instead of being filed separately. Two pre-fork events are real history the films build on: the Declaration of Independence, whose date the counterattack keeps, and the atomic bomb, which fails against the invaders' shields. Tiers: T4 holds 1776; T3 holds 1945-1998; T2 holds 2001-2016; T1 is empty.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs with the near-future branches because its fork is a dated event in our own calendar's next century, an alien invasion, and everything after it grows out of that one contact: a world government, a child army, a genocide and the guilt that follows. The continuity is Card's novels: Ender's Game and its direct sequels (Speaker for the Dead, Xenocide, Children of the Mind), with dates taken from the prequel Formic Wars trilogies and the Shadow and Exile books, which Card wrote into the same timeline. The 2013 film and the comics are not used. The CE years come from the Enderverse wiki's conversion, which rests on two years the books state. Coverage: T4 and T3 are empty except for the 1985 publication, because the story's history starts in the twenty-second century. T2 holds the Formic Wars and their aftermath (2115-2245). T1 holds the Speaker era three thousand years on (5268-5382), where every date depends on a calendar offset and is marked low.

events.title: Buenos Aires destroyed: the Bug War
events.description: After years of 'incidents' and 'police actions' as the Federation and the Arachnids expand into each other's space, the Bugs destroy Buenos Aires, killing Rico's mother. The first counter-stroke, Operation Bughouse against the Bug home world Klendathu, is a disaster.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs with the near-future branches because in 1959 its fork was a near future, a 1987 war and the end-of-century collapse behind it, and the society it builds out of that collapse is the book's whole argument. The continuity is Heinlein's novel only, not the 1997 film or its sequels and animation, which invent their own history. The dates rest on thin evidence: one stated year (1987), two relative phrases ('the end of the XXth century', 'a generation or two'), and Wikipedia's 'approximately 700 years in the future' for Rico's war, so everything after 2000 is low confidence. Coverage: T3 holds the fork and the wars of the late twentieth century. T2 holds the collapse and the founding of the Federation. The Bug War sits in T2 as well, in the 2660s. T4 and T1 are empty because the novel says nothing earlier than its 1987 war and nothing after Rico's last drop.

divergence.label: The future reaches back to 2015
divergence.delta: Real: 2015. The Brexit referendum and the US election are a year off, and the future is a matter for forecasters. Fiction: someone in 2136 sends information back to 2015 and splits off a branch of history, in which Britain votes to remain and Hillary Clinton becomes president.
divergence.inUniverse: The earliest stub contact, dated 2015 in Agency
divergence.note: Gibson's future can reach its own past by sending information through a server, and every contact splits off a new branch, a 'stub', whose future no longer leads to the contacting present. The fork is the earliest point at which any history in the books leaves ours: Agency's stub, split off in 2015. The branch that leads to the jackpot and Wilf's London is, by implication, our own history carried forward: Agency's stub differs from it at the 2016 referendum and election, so the root had the outcomes we had, and it is the one the meddlers came from. Flynne's world is a second stub, split off when London contacts it around 2030.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs with the near-future branches because the books branch history literally: each contact from the future splits off a 'stub', starting from 2015, a year we have lived through. The continuity is Gibson's two novels (The Peripheral, 2014; Agency, 2020), not the 2022 Amazon series. The lineage puts three strands on one calendar, and each note names its strand. Verity's stub, 2015-2017, is the Agency plot. Flynne's stub, about 2030 onward, is The Peripheral's American half. The root timeline is the jackpot and London, about 2040-2136. Only 2017 and 2136 are years the books state; the rest are derived and low. Coverage is T2 only (2014-2136). There is no T3 or T4 because nothing before 2015 differs from our history, and no T1 because the books never go past 2136.
